title: Air France Just Made Its Cheapest Awards Worse—My Plan To Beat The Devaluation And ...
description:
Air France KLM Flying Blue is making its cheapest awards worse beginning September 8.
Why I Actually Want Flying Blue Platinum The latest Frequent Miler On The Air does an excellent job laying out shortcuts to Flying Blue status.
You’ll often see 60,000 miles in business class when members without status see 142,000 miles or more.
Flying Blue Status Is Stupidly Complex I genuinely don’t know how the median Frenchman could possibly figure this out?
Bilt Platinum members get 12 months of Flying Blue Gold after transferring 10,000 Bilt points to Flying Blue.
text:
Air France KLM Flying Blue is making its cheapest awards worse beginning September 8. The lowest-priced awards will become “Light” fares: no changes, no refunds, fewer checked bags, paid advance seat assignments and, remarkably, no lounge access even when redeeming for business class.

You can pay more miles for a Standard award that restores most of what the same number of miles buys today, or still more for a Flex award. In Flying Blue’s New York – Paris business class example:

Light costs 60,000 miles plus $608.83.

Standard costs 75,000 miles plus $608.83.

Flex costs 110,000 miles plus $302.82.

So this is effectively a 25% increase if you want today’s ordinary award benefits. One importance nuance though is that elite benefits still apply to Light awards. Silver restores baggage and seat selection benefits. Gold restores lounge access. Platinum also provides free award changes and refunds. That turns elite status into a way of opting out of most of the devaluation.

I already have Flying Blue Gold through a Bilt status match. Now I plan to pursue Platinum because of two additional benefits.

Why I Actually Want Flying Blue Platinum

The latest Frequent Miler On The Air does an excellent job laying out shortcuts to Flying Blue status. Gold has already been useful to me for priority boarding, free checked bags and free exit row seats when flying Delta. Platinum adds more baggage, free award changes and refunds. But the two things I care about are:

Better award availability. The difference in saver award space is significant. You’ll often see 60,000 miles in business class when members without status see 142,000 miles or more. This matters even more when booking several seats for a family.

Ability to redeem for Air France La Première first class. These awards are still expensive and scarce. And they only allow one seat per flight currently. Ben Smith hates mileage redemption for first class. But it’s one of the world’s best overall passenger experiences, including the first class lounge in Paris.

Under the new system, Platinum can book the cheapest Light award, receive status-based bags, seats and lounge access, and still change or cancel without charge. A 60,000 mile Light award effectively becomes a 110,000 mile Flex award (albeit with the standard cash surcharge). And it has better availability. And I can book first class.

Flying Blue Status Is Stupidly Complex

I genuinely don’t know how the median Frenchman could possibly figure this out? Flying Blue awards Experience Points, generally abbreviated as XP, toward status. Starting without status, you need:

100 XP for Silver;

then another 180 XP for Gold; and

then another 300 XP for Platinum.

Each threshold is deducted when you reach it and a new 12-month qualification period begins. You therefore need 580 XP to go from nothing to Platinum. You cannot simply earn 300 XP for Platinum.

But a status match changes the equation. Bilt Platinum members get 12 months of Flying Blue Gold after transferring 10,000 Bilt points to Flying Blue. You receive the 10,000 Flying Blue miles (it’s not a status fee). And while the partnership lasts, the benefit can be re-upped each year. Mine recently expired and I’m purposely waiting to re-up.

The match gives you gold. It doesn’t give you XP. But once you are Gold, Platinum is earned with 300 XP in the upcoming 12 months. Flying Blue has also has a paid status match to Gold for $199. With Flying Blue, timing is everything.

The Bank Of America Card Gets Me 260 Of The 300 XP

The $89-annual-fee Air France KLM Visa Signature Card, whose improved status-earning structure I explained earlier this year, currently offers 70,000 miles and 100 XP after $3,000 in purchases during the first 90 days. It also provides:

20 XP each account anniversary

an additional 80 XP at the anniversary after spending $15,000 during the card year, and

another 60 XP after spending $25,000 during the card year.

That is 160 anniversary XP after $25,000 in total spending (not $25,000 on top of the first $15,000). Combined with the 100 XP initial bonus offer, the card can produce 260 XP during its first year. Starting from matched Gold, that leaves just 40 XP for Platinum.

The card earns 3 miles per dollar on Air France KLM and SkyTeam airlines (Delta, i.e. earns more on Delta tickets than buying with a Delta card does) and dining, 3 miles per dollar on rent paid through Bilt up to $50,000 per year (for a fee), and 1.5 miles per dollar elsewhere. I can earn 2 transferable points per dollar on other cards, so there is a real opportunity cost to putting $25,000 here.

The Timing Trick That Makes This Work

If the 100-XP welcome bonus posts while I have no status, Flying Blue will use those points to grant Silver and deduct them from my account. They will no longer be available for the climb from Gold to Platinum.

But the 160 XP from annual spending doesn’t post as the spending occurs. It arrives at or shortly after the card anniversary. If I activate the Bilt Gold match before opening the card, the matched status can expire before those anniversary points arrive. Then they don’t help for Platinum. So the way to do this is:

Apply for the Bank of America card first.

Don’t immediately complete the initial bonus offer spending.

Wait ~ 60 to 75 days after opening the card before activating a new Bilt Gold match. (creating a buffer between the first card anniversary and the end of the matched qualification year, allowing time for the anniversary XP to post).

Once Flying Blue shows Gold again, finish the $3,000 spending requirement before day 90. (The 100 initial XP should hit my Gold account rather than being consumed to create Silver.)

Spend $25,000 total during the cardmember year. (The first $3,000 is included in that amount.)

Earn another 40 XP before the matched Gold qualification period closes.

Once the 160 anniversary XP arrives, I should have 300 XP and move to Platinum – but it’ll take about a year from the time I get approved for the card. That doesn’t hit when you reach $25,000 spend, but after your cardmember anniversary. So needlessly complicated.

How To Earn The Missing 40 XP

I have several options, and the best answer is to combine activities I would undertake anyway.

Credit paid SkyTeam flights to Flying Blue. XP depends upon cabin, distance band and segments rather than ticket price. Connections can be valuable, and short international business class flights are disproportionately rewarding. For example, a paid Delta first class roundtrip from Austin to Canada or Mexico via a U.S. hub should earn 42 XP: 6 XP for each domestic segment and 15 XP for each short international segment.

Link Flying Blue with Accor Live Limitless. I haven’t previously used the partnership bonus offer, so the first eligible Accor stay after linking earns 5 XP and the first eligible Air France or KLM flight earns another 5 XP.

Contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel. Flying Blue awards 1 XP for each €10 contributed on an eligible Air France or KLM booking. Forty XP therefore costs about €400, or €300 after collecting the 10 Accor XP. The XP posts after the flight departs, and the contribution can be attached to an award booking even though the award flight itself doesn’t earn XP.

Donate Flying Blue miles to charity. Every 2,000 miles donated earns 1 XP, credited immediately. Forty XP would require 80,000 miles. That is a terrible value compared with €400 of sustainable fuel, but useful on an emergency basis right before a qualification deadline.

Buy an Air France Discount Pass. A new subscription or renewal comes with 20 XP and 2,500 or 5,000 miles. This is not cheaper than buying sustainable fuel solely for XP, but it can make sense for someone who will use the pass benefits.

Can I Reach Platinum Without Waiting A Year?

The frustrating part of this plan is waiting for the 160 card-spending XP to post at the first anniversary. Spending $25,000 quickly does not accelerate it. I’d probably do this with housing, quarterly tax or property tax payments (all of which come at a cost).

After receiving the 100 initial XP, I could reach Platinum earlier by producing the remaining 200 XP through paid flying, €2,000 of sustainable-fuel contributions, 400,000 donated miles, or some combination. Two well-routed paid business class trips between the United States and Europe with connecting segments can generate roughly 200 XP.

Another possibility raised by Frequent Miler is holding two Bank of America Flying Blue cards. If Bank of America approves two accounts and each awards the full anniversary XP, spending $25,000 on each would generate 320 XP annually, enough to maintain Platinum without flying. The terms limit a member to one new-account XP bonus every 24 months but appear to contemplate multiple accounts. I’d love to hear from readers that have tried this.

Generally you can open up to 2 BofA cards in 2 months, no more than in a year, and no more than 4 in two years. And they won’t usually approve cardmembers who have 3 or more new accounts open with any issuer in the past 12 months (though if you have a deposit account with them it’s 7 accounts in 12 months) however I’ve seen mixed data points on this guideline.

Earning Platinum Once Is Easier Than Keeping It

The first-year card bonus gets me to 260 XP. In subsequent years, one card provides only 160 XP after $25,000 in spending, leaving 140 XP per year to maintain Platinum.

That can come from paid flying, sustainable fuel contributions, a second card or a mixture. If I don’t requalify, Flying Blue provides a soft landing to Gold rather than dropping me to the bottom. Earning Platinum once therefore gives me a year of Platinum followed by at least a year of Gold, and potentially Silver after that. Ten consecutive years of Platinum earns Platinum for life.

I wouldn’t normally recommend chasing airline status for benefits that can be purchased more cheaply. I don’t value this for the checked bags and seat assignments and lounge access. I get those already. But savings on redemptions for my full family, which I’ll do with Air France at least once a year but given the savings it’s probably four seats times two trips.

text:
New aviation technologies ranging from electric air taxis and autonomous aircraft to medical delivery drones and advanced airport planning tools are creating opportunities across Illinois. Those opportunities, and their potential to take off in St. Louis’ Metro East, were highlighted by Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT) officials during a presentation at the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit held August 19 and 20 in O’Fallon, Illinois.

Presented by BJ Murray, Section Chief of Aviation Transportation Program Planning for IDOT, and Todd Dugan, Aviation Annual Program Planning Specialist for IDOT, the session highlighted statewide studies examining advanced air mobility (AAM), airport operations tracking and aviation's growing role in supporting economic development, transportation innovation and future infrastructure investment.

Much of the discussion focused on how Illinois is preparing for a new era of aviation that extends well beyond traditional passenger air travel. Through its Advanced Air Mobility System Plan Study, IDOT is evaluating infrastructure, airspace and policy considerations needed to support emerging technologies such as electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, autonomous systems and drone-based operations. The study examines how emerging aviation technologies are beginning to reshape transportation, logistics, healthcare, agriculture and aerospace manufacturing, while highlighting the Metro East region’s role in that evolution.

"We recognized that other states were beginning to lay the groundwork and Illinois was falling behind in planning for this new technology," Dugan said. "The purpose of the study is to recognize and prioritize existing and near-term advanced air mobility opportunities from an infrastructure, airspace and IDOT policy perspective."

Panelists noted that advanced air mobility is already moving from concept to reality. Companies across the aviation industry are working toward certification of passenger-carrying electric aircraft, while drone technologies are being deployed for medical deliveries, package distribution and agricultural applications. IDOT's planning efforts are intended to help ensure Illinois is prepared to accommodate and benefit from those innovations as they expand.

The session highlighted examples already being tested around the world and in Illinois. Medical drone systems have been used to transport blood and critical supplies to remote communities in Rwanda, while Northwestern Medicine in Chicago has explored drone-based transportation of medical samples. Retail and logistics companies continue expanding drone delivery programs, and agricultural operators are evaluating autonomous aircraft capable of supporting around-the-clock field operations.

Presenters also pointed to significant aviation innovation already taking place in the Metro East. Dugan cited Boeing's MQ-25 Stingray program at MidAmerica St. Louis Airport as an example of next-generation aerospace technology being developed in the region.

"This technology is not just the technology of the future. It is the technology of the present. Look no further than MidAmerica St. Louis Airport and what Boeing is doing with the MQ-25,” Dugan said. “It's great to see the Metro East leading the charge in some of these new cases.”

As advanced air mobility evolves, presenters said Illinois airports are expected to play an important role in supporting early deployment of new aircraft, while future infrastructure may include specialized vertiports located near urban centers, transit facilities and major destinations. These facilities would require new planning approaches as well as electrical infrastructure capable of supporting aircraft charging systems.

The discussion also highlighted a statewide airport operations counting initiative that uses Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) technology to provide more accurate aircraft activity data. The information helps airport planners better understand how runways, taxiways and other facilities are used, supporting airport master plans, environmental reviews and future capital investments.

Murray noted that improved operational data can strengthen planning efforts and help airports secure funding for infrastructure projects by providing a clearer picture of aviation activity and facility utilization.

"This new technology has much more usage and is much more accurate,” Murray said. “It helps to justify capital developments at individual airports and within the system and show how our aviation infrastructure is being used."

The session also provided context on the scale of Illinois' aviation system. According to IDOT, the state's airports generate approximately $95.5 billion in annual economic impact, support nearly 500,000 jobs and connect Illinois to 48 states, 73 countries and five continents. IDOT is currently updating that economic impact analysis – something they do every five years - with new findings expected to be released in spring 2027 after completion of ongoing data collection and analysis efforts.

For the St. Louis Metro East region, MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, St. Louis Downtown Airport and St. Louis Regional Airport collectively generate more than $4 billion annually in economic impact, with significant expansion occurring at each facility since the last statewide study was completed. Presenters noted that upcoming updates are expected to include higher numbers reflecting the continued growth and investment throughout the region's aviation sector.

The second annual Global Aerospace Summit brought together aerospace manufacturers, suppliers and leaders in military, cargo movement, transportation, economic development and related industries for a two-day program focused on innovation, collaboration and growth. The event was presented by the Leadership Council Southwestern Illinois; Madison County, Illinois; St. Clair County, Illinois, and Bi-State Development's St. Louis Regional Freightway.

title: What We Carry Forward - Seed World
description:
Our cover story follows her work helping seed companies navigate labeling requirements across 50 states.
Seed companies cannot build production plans around enthusiasm alone.
That idea stayed with me because it reflects a broader shift across the seed industry.
Breeders, seed companies and researchers are being asked to understand not only how a crop performs, but where it goes and what people need from it.
What we carry forward — our experience, our relationships and our willingness to keep learning — will shape how well we answer.
text:
Every magazine issue looks different when it is still spread across a screen or a desk.

There are interview notes, half-finished headlines, photo selections, page proofs and stories that do not seem connected yet. Then something begins to emerge. Not a planned theme, necessarily, but a question that keeps showing up in different forms.

For the Seed World U.S. September issue (that should be in your mailbox really soon), that question was simple: What does it take to move an idea into the real world? The answer is almost never innovation alone.

The Details That Make It Work

Karen Withers understands that better than many.

Our cover story follows her work helping seed companies navigate labeling requirements across 50 states. It is detailed, exacting work. A word that is acceptable in one state may create a problem in another. A label can become outdated. A requirement can change. Something that looks minor on paper can delay a product or expose a company to risk.

I have always been drawn to the people who understand those hidden parts of an industry. They know where the complications live. More important, they know how to help others move through them.

Karen’s work may not attract the same attention as artificial intelligence or gene editing, but the industry needs it just as much. A breakthrough cannot create value if it cannot make its way through the systems surrounding it.

That lesson appears throughout this issue.

Sustainable aviation fuel could open an entirely new market for agriculture. The possibility is enormous: crops, residues and purpose-grown feedstocks helping fuel commercial flight. But farmers cannot plant possibility. Seed companies cannot build production plans around enthusiasm alone. The economics, genetics, infrastructure and demand all have to line up.

The opportunity is real. So are the unanswered questions.

Faster Is Not the Same as Finished

The same tension appears in our story about artificial intelligence and corn breeding.

Virtual fields give researchers the ability to evaluate plant architecture and test ideas before committing years and acres to field trials. That changes what breeders can consider and how quickly they can narrow their choices.

Still, corn eventually has to grow in actual soil, under actual heat, wind, disease and drought. The technology does not replace the breeder or the field. It gives them a better place to begin.

Gene editing has reached a similar point. Scientists can now make precise changes with speed that would have seemed remarkable not long ago. Commercialization has not caught up. Regulatory decisions, testing, public understanding and value-chain coordination still take time.

That gap matters. We often talk about innovation as though discovery marks the finish line. In practice, discovery may be where the harder work begins.

Weather can widen that gap even further. Shawn Hackett’s warning about a possible super El Niño is not simply a forecast story. It is a planning story. A major weather shift can alter production, commodity markets, regional demand and seed supply long before anyone knows exactly how the season will unfold.

Companies cannot control that uncertainty. They can decide whether they prepare for it.

A Broader Definition of Progress

One story in this issue asks plant breeders to consider an even bigger question: Who are they breeding for?

USDA leaders are encouraging researchers to think beyond traditional agronomic performance and consider nutrition, human health, consumer preferences and the needs of the entire food system. Yield will always matter. So will standability, disease resistance and performance under stress.

But the crop’s job does not end at harvest.

That idea stayed with me because it reflects a broader shift across the seed industry. The work now touches more people, more markets and more expectations than it once did. Breeders, seed companies and researchers are being asked to understand not only how a crop performs, but where it goes and what people need from it.

None of that makes the traditional work less important. It makes the connections more visible.

When I look across these stories, I do not see a collection of unrelated technologies, markets and challenges. I see an industry carrying knowledge forward while learning when it must adapt.

That knowledge lives in people. It lives in the breeder who knows what a model cannot see, the regulatory expert who catches one problematic word, the company watching a weather pattern before it becomes a crisis and the researcher willing to ask whether an old definition of success is still enough.

Those are not always the loudest parts of progress. They are often the parts that make progress possible.

The future will continue to ask more of this industry. What we carry forward — our experience, our relationships and our willingness to keep learning — will shape how well we answer.

It’s been an honor to partner with you,

Aimee

“This new tool gives travellers the opportunity to help increase the use of SAF and support more sustainable air travel.” SAF is a lower-carbon alternative to fossil jet fuel.

text:
As part of its commitment to sustainability and reducing carbon emissions, Vancouver International Airport (YVR) – a Corporate Partner of the FTE Digital, Innovation & Startup Hub – has launched a new tool for passengers to be part of the transition to a lower-carbon aviation industry. YVR’s online calculator allows travellers to estimate their flight’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and contribute to the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

Contributions made through YVR’s new online calculator will be applied to environmental attributes associated with SAF and will enable airlines’ further use of SAF, starting with Air Canada. SAF’s environmental attributes are the quantified climate benefits or reductions associated with its use, such as the GHG emissions avoided by not extracting non-renewable resources used for fossil jet fuel. Contributing to these attributes supports SAF growth and is essential for scaling SAF globally, as it bolsters activity across the supply chain.

“Sustainable Aviation Fuel is one of the most effective options available today to make meaningful progress towards decarbonising aviation,” said Tamara Vrooman, President & CEO, Vancouver International Airport. “This new tool gives travellers the opportunity to help increase the use of SAF and support more sustainable air travel.”

SAF is a lower-carbon alternative to fossil jet fuel. It is made from renewable and waste-derived materials and, depending on the feedstock, production pathway and lifecycle-assessment methodology, can have lower lifecycle GHG emissions than fossil jet fuel. Certain SAF may achieve lifecycle GHG reductions of up to 80% when used in neat form compared with fossil jet fuel. As a ‘drop-in’ fuel, it can be blended with fossil jet fuel and requires no changes to today’s aircraft or existing airport infrastructure.

While SAF is currently in use by some airlines, including those operating at YVR, as an emerging fuel source, limited production and higher prices are obstacles for wider uptake. As production increases and more supply becomes available, costs are likely to lower, increasing the proportion of SAF to be likely used in flights around the world.

This initiative is part of YVR’s broader efforts to raise awareness of SAF and support airline partners in increasing their SAF use to advance the aviation industry’s goal of net zero emissions by 2050. While voluntary contributions through YVR’s online calculator help support the broader adoption of SAF by Air Canada over time, the tool is available to all passengers regardless of which airline they travel on.

Nu Quantum, Cisco, NTT Data, OQC (Oxford Quantum Circuits), QphoX, Quantinuum and QuEra established the QDA in 2025 with the mission of bringing together leading voices from the quantum computing and data center communities to address one of the field’s most pressing bottlenecks: how to integrate emerging quantum hardware into existing and future data center infrastructure. As quantum systems move from lab-scale demonstrations toward commercial deployment, questions about system-level architecture, control, error correction, interoperability and power consumption have become as critical as the qubits themselves.

“Cross-industry collaboration is essential to delivering utility-scale quantum computers,” said Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, CEO of Nu Quantum. “The QDA provides a vital space for the leading companies in our ecosystem to exchange ideas and accelerate the progress needed to make this technology a reality.”

The one-day event will focus on a single question: how to build datacenter-scale quantum computers and accelerate the timeline to fault-tolerance. Sessions will cover the full computing stack (quantum processors, interconnects, entanglement networks, middleware, system integration, software, algorithms, and applications), reflecting the QDA’s premise that no single organization can solve this alone. The day’s speakers include:

Dame Wendy Hall, Regius Professor at the University of Southampton and the inventor of Microcosm, the precursor to the World Wide Web

Dr. Ben Bloom, CEO of Atom Computing

Dr. Alexei Bylinskii, VP of Quantum Computing Services, QuEra Computing

Dr. Anna Tatarczak, Distinguished Member of Technical Staff at Coherent Inc., specializing in next-generation data center interconnects

Andy Grant, EMEA Director, Supercomputing, Higher Education, and AI at NVIDIA

Jim Sexton, Fellow at IBM

Michael Hush, Chief Scientist at Q-CTRL

Dr. Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, CEO of Nu Quantum

Dr. Karmela Padavic-Callaghan, journalist covering physics, materials science and quantum technology at New Scientist

Seyon Sivarajah, Chief Architect for Developer Tools at Quantinuum

Registration for the Forum is open, but capacity at the venue is limited. The QDA is curating the attendee list to facilitate the kind of close, cross-disciplinary exchange that a smaller room makes possible: prioritizing depth of expertise and diversity of perspective across the quantum networking stack.

Robert Stockill, CTO at QphoX, said: “With so many pioneers in quantum data centre design and implementation gathered at the QDA Forum, we have a unique chance to understand the very edge of technological advancement in scalable quantum computing, and stimulate the next round of innovation in these powerful and rapidly evolving systems.”

“Realizing the full potential of quantum technology and its role in the future of compute involves deploying it directly into AI data centers to operate in hybrid capacities alongside classical HPC environments,” said Dr. Jennifer Strabley, Corporate Vice President and General Manager of the Compute Platform Group at Quantinuum. “This global alliance provides the collaborative foundation necessary to address the system-level challenges required to accelerate scalable interoperability in alignment with the public and private sector leaders across the ecosystem.”

HONG KONG, Aug. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The seventh edition of ReThink HK, Hong Kong's flagship climate action and sustainable business event, will open on 10–11 September at Hall 1, HKCEC. Restructured around five dedicated Thematic Zones — Cities, Energy, Impact, Innovation, and Resources — the event is expected to convene 10,000+ attendees, 500+ speakers, and 350+ solution providers as Asia's business sector shifts from climate target-setting to operational delivery. The restructured format is designed to help business leaders convert ESG strategies into operational results amid intensifying regulatory pressure globally.

Since 2020, attendance has grown more than 12-fold - a 1,150% increase in six years. Nearly one-third of attendees hold board-level or sustainability leadership roles, reflecting the event's position as a decision-maker forum for the region's net-zero transition.

Streamlining Climate Action: The 5 Thematic Zones

"As companies transition from setting climate targets to executing operational roadmaps, the demand for practical, scalable solutions has never been higher," said Mr. Chris Brown, Founder & CEO of ReThink HK. "We have restructured the entire conference around five thematic zones to help business leaders forge meaningful partnerships and convert ESG strategies into measurable business value."

The Cities Zone targets actionable solutions in sustainable infrastructure, green building technologies and liveable urban engineering for Asia's densely populated cities.

The Energy Zone explores the region's evolving energy ecosystem, from renewable integration and grid decarbonisation to sustainable aviation fuel, clean maritime fuels and the electrification of transport.

The Impact Zone convenes strategic ESG governance, green finance for SMEs, social value creation and community-level climate action.

The Innovation Zone features cutting-edge climate technology, AI-driven sustainability tools and the university spinout and startup ecosystems commercialising research into deployable solutions.

The Resources Zone presents circular economy solutions, waste reduction innovation and sustainable materials management across Asia's manufacturing and supply chain networks.

Global Innovations & AI-Powered Networking

Cross-Sector Coalitions Turning Commitments into Delivery

ReThink HK 2026 continues to receive strong endorsement from the HKSAR Government, underscoring a unified public-private effort to advance Hong Kong's climate goals. text: SUSTAINABLE AVIATION FUEL "SAF" UNSUSTAINABLE for passengers and airlines: The airline industry has a plan to buy 500 million tonnes of alternative jet fuel "SAF" a year by 2050. Its own study of that plan says a techno-economic assessment was outside the scope of the work. They did not price it. So I did. About 1.9 trillion dollars a year. The working is in the image. Europe's aviation regulator has to publish reference prices for every fuel in its mandate, because the penalty for missing the mandate is set at twice the gap to kerosene. EASA cannot fine anyone without a number. Lay IATA's plan over those prices. > The cheapest route, fats and oils, is capped at 63 million tonnes. > Agroforestry residues carry 108 million at four times kerosene. > Synthetic fuel carries 176 million at twelve times cost of kerosene. Two thirds of the plan sits in the two dearest categories on the list. One thing to pin down before the multiplication. IATA needs 500 million tonnes; its own core forecast delivers 412. I have priced the 412, because that is the mix IATA publishes. Pricing the shortfall would make the number bigger, not smaller. 412 million tonnes at a premium of about USD 4,610 a tonne is roughly 1.9 trillion dollars a year. Every year. If you think I have loaded the mix, use IATA's own figure instead. It says 2.4 million tonnes of this fuel cost airlines an extra USD 4.3 billion in 2026. About USD 1,800 a tonne. Hold today's mix constant, change nothing but volume, and 2050 costs USD 740 billion a year. That is the floor, and it is their arithmetic. For scale: IATA expects the entire global airline industry to turn over USD 1.165 trillion in 2026, at a 2.0% net margin, for a profit of USD 23 billion. The premium is: >> 1.6 times industry revenue >> more than five times its fuel bill >> over eighty times its profit. That is not a subsidy figure. It is a cost premium, and premiums split between fares, airline margin and public money. But an industry earning 23 billion cannot absorb 1.9 trillion. So it goes to passengers or to treasuries, and IATA's study already says which it assumes: financial support mechanisms, market incentives or carbon pricing, assumed to be in place. Two caveats I would rather state than have quoted at me. Only kerosene and fats & oils are real market prices; everything above four times is EASA modelling a hypothetical first plant, because those fuels are barely made. And synthetic fuel was absent from the European fuel mix entirely in 2024. So the question was never whether this is possible. Anything with a cost is possible. The question is: WHO PAYS ? A target with no cost model is not a plan. It is a hope like all net-zero dreams. Continued in comments. Sources: EASA, 2025 Aviation Fuels Reference Prices for ReFuelEU Aviation. IATA and Worley Consulting, Global Feedstock Assessment for SAF Production, September 2025. IATA industry outlook, 2026-06-07.

text:
From water, renewable electricity, and carbon dioxide from sustainable sources, high-quality, climate-neutral aviation fuel is to be created. This is the goal of researchers at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI in collaboration with the Zurich-based company Metafuels. On 20 August 2026 their innovative project bringing science and industry together became tangible with the inauguration of the “aerobrew” demonstration plant on the PSI campus. More than 150 guests from science, politics, industry, and the energy sector attended the inauguration ceremony, including Dieter Egli, a member of the Aargau cantonal government; Francine Zimmermann, director of the Federal Office of Civil Aviation; and Jens Fehlinger, CEO of Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS).

With the new demonstration plant, the emerging “aerobrew” technology is now being operated for the first time in an industrially relevant plant design. This is a novel catalytic process for producing synthetic aeroplane fuel – known as SAF, for sustainable aviation fuel – that PSI researchers and the Metafuels team jointly developed and patented. The project combines scientific research with industrial development in a targeted way to transform new findings into practical applications.

Aviation safety: Rapid test for harmful microbes in kerosene developed

Faster and more robust than a PCR test

Read news

“At PSI, we conduct research for society. The energy transition is one of the major challenges we are currently facing,” says PSI Director Christian Rüegg. “The inauguration of the ‘aerobrew’ demonstration plant is an important milestone on the path to more sustainable aviation. We are proud that our cutting-edge research is making a crucial contribution to this step towards industrial production.”

From green methanol to sustainable fuel

“We have successfully developed ‘aerobrew’ together with Metafuels on a laboratory scale. With our demonstration plant, we are now testing the process under real-world conditions,” says Marco Ranocchiari, a researcher at the PSI Center for Energy and Environmental Sciences, who leads PSI‘s involvement in the “aerobrew” project. “This will allow us to further optimise the technology and create the conditions for industrial production.”

“International travel and global supply chains will continue to depend on air transport,” explains Saurabh Kapoor, co-founder and CEO of Metafuels. “That’s why we have developed a product that can be integrated into existing airport infrastructure and used in conventional jet engines, while at the same time significantly reducing climate-damaging emissions.” Metafuels plans to bring the first commercial plant for production of SAF using the “aerobrew” technology into operation starting in 2030.

The “aerobrew” process requires no fossil fuels and achieves higher selectivity – a better yield-to-revenue ratio – compared to previously used production methods for SAF. The source materials are water, from which hydrogen is produced using sustainable electricity, and carbon dioxide. The latter can in the short term be sourced from biogenic sources such as wood or plant waste, and in the long term directly from the atmosphere. Hydrogen and carbon dioxide are processed into green methanol. Finally, the “aerobrew” technology comes into play: it generates sustainable kerosene from the green methanol.

text: Wellington Airport has released its annual Kaitiakitanga report showing a 29% drop in gross emissions since 2017 as part of its annual climate and environmental reporting. This includes Scope 1 and 2 emissions and business travel. When certified renewable energy is included, direct emissions (Scope 1 and 2) have decreased by 77% since 2017. This puts the airport well on track for its target of net sero emissions for Scope 1 and 2 by 2030, with the replacement of gas boilers in 2028 expected to bring the total close to 100%. A key part of this is setting clear goals and publishing regular updates on how we’re tracking. Emissions from aircraft themselves are still clearly the biggest challenge, but we are making progress in that area too. Airlines are operating more fuel-efficient aircraft at Wellington, and we proudly hosted Air New Zealand’s first electric aircraft last summer.” The emissions progress is a highlight of Wellington Airport’s annual Kaitiakitanga report which summarises the airport’s environmental and social efforts. Other highlights over the past 12 months include: Fast-track approval for southern seawall renewal; Founding member of the New Zealand Sustainable Aviation Fuel Industry Roundtable; Successful feasibility study paving way for replacement of gas boilers; Solar panels installed on roof of new Airport Fire Station; 23% of available seat kilometres operated by next-generation fuel efficient aircraft (compared with 9% in 2020); Sponsorship of nearly every major Wellington event and support for local causes including Predator Free Wellington. INDIANAPOLIS — The Indiana Corn Marketing Council (ICMC) and the Indiana Corn Growers Association (ICGA) are delighted to see Indiana-grown corn once again playing a role in the future of INDYCAR racing through Shell’s updated 100 percent Renewable Race Fuel, which will debut during the 2027 NTT INDYCAR SERIES season.

“This is great news for Indiana farmers,” said J.R. Roesner, ICGA Board Member and corn farmer from Ferdinand, Ind. “Ethanol is a major industry in our state and accounts for more than 40 percent of our corn grind. It’s exciting to see a homegrown, renewable fuel from Indiana become part of the fuel powering INDYCAR race cars.”

On its website, INDYCAR reported the updated Shell 100 percent Renewable Race Fuel is expected to deliver at least a 70 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared with the Renewable Fuel Standard average gasoline baseline. The fuel will continue to meet the performance and durability requirements of INDYCAR and its engine manufacturers.

For Indiana corn farmers, seeing their crop and its renewable products showcased in innovative competitions like motorsports is another example of the diverse markets created by Indiana’s corn industry.

State Rep. J.D. Prescott (R-Union City), also an ICMC Board member, applauded Friday’s announcement. Nearly one year ago, Prescott called on INDYCAR to source its ethanol from Indiana, urging the racing series to support American farmers and domestic ethanol producers.

“Racing is a part of Indiana’s heritage, so it makes sense that the fuel powering these incredible race cars should support Hoosier farmers and workers,” Prescott said. “I’m proud to see INDYCAR make this change, bringing the purchase of ethanol back home. This decision will support Indiana’s corn farmers, strengthen our ethanol industry and benefit our state’s economy.”

This result could not have happened without the combined efforts of ICGA and ICMC. While ICGA campaigned state and federal lawmakers for more opportunities to expand Indiana’s ethanol industry, ICMC worked with ethanol producers to site new bioprocessing facilities throughout the state.

Indiana plants nearly 5.5 million acres of corn each year, and those acres yield more than 1 billion bushels. Indiana is the fifth-largest, corn-producing state in America. Corn farmers who work within 30 miles of one of the state’s 15 ethanol plant can realize an 18-23 cent per bushel premium on corn prices. At more than 1.4 billion gallons per year, Indiana is the fifth-largest U.S. producer of ethanol – accounting for nearly 8 percent of the total U.S. ethanol output.

“Since its creation in 2007, the Indiana Corn Marketing Council has worked diligently in making sure the infrastructure was in place so that Hoosier farmers could benefit from the opportunities of an expanding ethanol market,” said ICMC President Susan Brocksmith, a corn farmer from Vincennes, Ind. “This announcement is another success story from that work. Without the efforts of bringing 15 ethanol biorefineries into Indiana, we may not have had the ability to fulfill the needs to supply INDYCAR’s racing fuel needs.”

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel Pioneer Completes Successful Trials

(Nova Pangea Technologies) Nova Pangaea Technologies, the UK company with a unique process to create sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from waste biomass, has completed successful endurance trials that further validate its technology.

Nova Pangaea Technologies, the UK company with a unique process to create ethanol and biochar from waste biomass for the production of carbon-negative sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), has completed successful endurance trials that further validate its technology.

The trials, which took place at its demonstration plant on Teesside, show continuous stable operation in production runs of up to 72 hours and achieved above target yields.

It marks another step forward for Nova Pangaea, which will be raising funds to progress its first commercial plant, and comes as the aviation industry seeks ways to scale up SAF production using other sustainable raw materials to end the current dependence on waste oils and fats.

Nova Pangaea is working with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird, an initiative supported by the UK government to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from local waste biomass to decarbonise the aviation sector. For Speedbird, Nova Pangaea will construct four UK facilities to produce bioethanol from local wastes for upgrading to SAF via LanzaJet’s Alcohol-to-Jet biorefinery.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts waste biomass and residues, such as wood chips, sawdust, or wheat straw, into ethanol, which can be used to make SAF and renewable diesel. It also produces a valuable co-product, biochar, which permanently captures carbon and makes the whole process carbon negative – removing more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases.

The latest trials used softwood residues from timber processing. Multiple runs were carried out processing up to 3 tonnes of feedstock per day.

They follow initial smaller-scale trials in early 2025 which demonstrated the viability of the process outside of the laboratory. More trials will take place next year to fine tune the design of the first commercial scale plant.

By enabling the use of waste biomass, Nova Pangaea’s process can help prevent potential shortages of SAF in the future. Under UK and EU rules, airlines must use an increasing proportion of SAF in aviation fuel – rising from 2% to as much as 70% in 2050. However, at present almost all SAF comes from used cooking oil, which is in limited supply and will not be enough to meet future demand.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), in 2030 there will be enough waste biomass available in Europe including the UK to produce around 30 million tonnes of SAF, equivalent to the European SAF targets for 2050.

Stewart Stewart, CEO of Nova Pangaea, said: “The latest trials have validated our technology and should further underpin the confidence of investors on our journey towards building our first commercial plant.

“The SAF industry is currently at a critical point. Demand is increasing and supply chain shocks such as in the Middle East show the need to find an alternative to fossil fuels, yet aviation is currently reliant on SAF from a single feedstock, which will not be enough to meet growing SAF demand.

“Nova Pangaea’s tried and tested technology offers a genuine alternative. By tapping into the plentiful supplies of waste biomass, we can boost SAF production – enhancing our energy security, and building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and revenues while reducing fossil fuel emissions.”

text:
Census figures show Hawaiʻi's population is aging faster than the national average. That's also an issue in many parts of Asia, where one government is trying a new approach to meet some of the challenges.

Singapore's government says the country has a baby problem: there aren’t enough of them.

The government wants to encourage its citizens to have more children to increase its birth rate and create a demographic cushion for its aging population.

And it's willing to spend more money to make that happen.

This past weekend, a key part of Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s National Day speech focused on child support.

The idea of a “baby bonus” at birth is not new — Singapore's government has paid one for the past 25 years.

Now, those payments will be increased — and spread out through the age of 17, including money to support the child's higher education.

Parental leave policies are also increasing, and more of the costs will be paid by the government instead of employers.

There’s even a portion related to housing.

But the Prime Minister himself says this isn't likely to by itself solve the population issue, which will continue to require immigration.

And there are mixed views from prospective parents.

A marketing firm called YouGov recently surveyed 500 young Singaporeans from their late teens to their mid-forties.

Nearly a third said there was nothing the government could do to incentivize them to have children.

description:

text:
I started noodling on this topic with the premise that the AI genie is out of its bottle and it ain’t going back in.* So, given the concerns around AI – jobs, IP rights, slop, poor quality, users being lazy, let alone environmental and community concerns around data centers – it got me thinking: How can the ad industry sustainably use AI in marketing?

Let’s find out.

Quigley-Simpson co-founder Gerald Bagg notes that, for the most part, the environmental impact of AI is not a “routine client question” yet.

“Most organizations remain more focused on capability, speed, cost, governance and accuracy. But environmental impact will become harder to ignore as AI moves from occasional experimentation to continuous production at scale,” Bagg says.

Neil Clark, chief sustainability officer of MSQ, parent of Big Spaceship, also says it’s not a top question from clients, but he expects more clients will start asking it.

“It’s a significant topic internally,” Clark adds. “Our people raise it regularly, they want to act on it and they push us to do better. That matters because our clients’ teams are made up of the same kind of people. If our own employees are asking these questions, theirs will be too.”

What is AI’s environmental impact?

While there is some data online about the energy usage required for AI prompts and creations, many of the big players do not disclose such details or are current with it.

Let’s start small: A typical interaction on OpenAI’s ChatGPT uses about 0.3 watt-hours of electricity. Since a standard LED light bulb uses 10 watts, that AI query equates to about 2 minutes of powering the bulb.

How about images? A generative AI image takes approximately 1.2 watt hours, or the same energy as having an LED light bulb on for 7 minutes.

Video? That can take 30 to 950 watt hours, depending on quality. Looking at the higher end, creating a generative AI video can equate to leaving that light bulb on for four days.

If we compound the above information across the entire industry, that’s A LOT of light bulbs with the switch on.

With that being said, the energy to process prompts is becoming more efficient. Google says that, in May 2024, the medium Gemini prompt used 33 times more energy than it did a year later. The tech giant says software optimization, including improvements in models, contributed to the increase in energy efficiency.

Note: Scroll to the bottom to see how Ad Net Zero’s Global Media Sustainability Framework and AdGreen help measure the ad industry’s AI-related emissions.

Do consumers want AI in their advertising?

A May Bentley University-Gallup Business in Society Survey showed that 73% of US adults don’t trust businesses (either not much or not at all) to responsibly use AI. While that’s an improvement from 2023 (78%), mistrust this year is up when compared to 2025 (69%).

Let’s get closer to marketing.

One in 5 millennials has a negative view of AI’s use in marketing, which soars to nearly 2 in 5 when you ask Generation Z, per an IAB study released earlier in 2026.

When seeking an emotional connection, generative AI may not be the way to go. Kantar found that, while generative AI-created ads can spark emotion in consumers, that emotion is often not what was intended and is negative.

How about the sought-after trust factor with consumers? Klaviyo found that 31% of global consumers put less trust in a brand that uses generative AI, though 61% were neutral.

Sustainable use of AI in marketing

Getting back to the premise, there are ways today to use AI in marketing that minimize its environmental impact.

“The biggest step that you can take is the call you never make,” MSQ’s Clark says. “Plenty of tasks don’t need an AI at all, and simply asking ‘does this actually need a model?’ avoids a surprising amount.”

Clark adds that, “When something does need AI, the next question is whether it’s going to the right model, which isn’t always the smallest one. A model that’s too weak for the job just sends you round in circles regenerating answers, and that wastes far more [energy] than choosing the capable option the first time.

“Equally, reaching for the most powerful model for a task [that] a lighter one could handle is poor practice.”

Quigley-Simpson’s Bagg echoes that approach, noting that strategic thought is needed when using AI tools.

“Avoid endless generation simply to produce more alternatives. Reuse approved outputs rather than recreating them. … Reserve highly computational tools, particularly image and video generation, for situations in which they create genuine value,” Bagg says.

Bagg also says agencies and clients need to expect more from their partners.

“Organizations should also ask their technology partners for greater transparency about energy use, data-center efficiency, model size and the source of the electricity supporting their systems. Marketers cannot manage what providers do not disclose,” he says.

Clark asserts that using task-specific AI tools may be more efficient than a “general purpose giant.”

His agency took this approach with MSQ Assist, an internal AI platform. MSQ Assist “routes each task to the most appropriate model rather than defaulting to the biggest. Assist is also built on our own knowledge of our clients and is heavily templated, so it steers people towards focused, well-structured prompts and processes rather than a blank box/page every time,” Clark explains.

Sustainable considerations for adland

Today and going forward, Clark says that there are two key reasons for thinking about sustainable use of AI in advertising.

The first is simple: “AI has a real and fast-growing energy and water footprint, and marketing is adopting it at pace, so the totals mount up quickly,” Clark says.

The second leans into the important role the marketing industry plays in society.

“Marketing doesn’t only consume energy, it shapes what people see as normal and desirable. If we use AI to manufacture over consumption, or we model wasteful, throwaway AI habits ourselves, we scale that behavior across millions of people. We could just as easily do the opposite.

“Therefore, AI’s impact isn’t only about our own footprint, it’s about whether an industry with this much influence chooses to use one of the most powerful tools it has ever had thoughtfully, or not,” Clark says.

The use of AI in marketing, Bagg says, also plays into a much broader question that agencies always need to ask”

“Did this work need to be created, and did it produce enough value to justify the resources consumed?

“The more consequential and potentially controversial argument is that responsible AI use may sometimes mean deciding not to use AI at all. That challenges the prevailing assumption that greater AI adoption is inherently progress, and it is a sufficiently distinct position to warrant attention,” Bagg says.

As Clark and Bagg point out, the question about sustainable AI in marketing is not so much about the use of AI, it goes to the foundational questions that must be asked at the start of projects: What do you want to accomplish and what’s the best way to do it. And, of course, you want to do it as effectively and efficiently as possible.

* As Generation Z gets more ingrained in the workforce, it will have a say in AI usage. Also, if you disagree or have thoughts on the premise, email me.

AI impact: Ad industry resources

There are three ways that Ad Net Zero’s Global Media Sustainability Framework captures emissions from AI use: Unit operations formulae, “asset manipulation” unit operations and “corporate overhead emissions” allocation.

Ad Net Zero Global Director Jo Fenn says the framework will likely expand from creative workflow to include media delivery, optimization and other ways, including AI as a media channel.

The AdGreen Carbon Calculator measures ad production emissions and, in 2025, rolled in AI measurement. The calculator includes an Early Insights component that enables marketers to gauge the emissions impact of creative choices before being finalized.

Fenn says the tools available offer a lot of potential. “What’s exciting – and challenging – is that these show us both progress and potential. The industry is measuring more production activity than ever before, but we know we’re still only seeing a small part of the picture. Every additional production measured unlocks opportunities to reduce more emissions and save more money – without compromising creativity.”

text:
(Nova Pangea Technologies) Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) offers the opportunity to reduce our dependence on imported fossil fuels, with the price volatility and the economic impact that brings, while at the same time reducing carbon emissions from air travel. Unlike conventional jet fuel, SAF can be made from more locally available feedstocks such as forestry and agricultural residues.

Yet despite the obvious benefits, SAF still represents only a tiny fraction of global aviation fuel use and the biggest obstacle to adoption is cost. As SAF is more expensive than conventional jet fuel, airlines are concerned that it will lead to higher ticket prices.

Some airlines are now challenging the government mandates that require jet fuel to contain an increasing proportion of SAF – currently over 3% in the UK and rising to 10% in 2030.

Yet herein lies the irony. The SAF mandates will boost demand and help encourage investment in new plants – and it is only by scaling up production that we can significantly improve efficiency and bring down costs. Without doing so, prices will remain higher, supplies will be limited and nations will be trapped in the oil shock doom loop.

Clearly the price of SAF is a barrier. But how much more expensive is it than fossil-based fuel, to what extent would it affect ticket prices and how could we bring down the cost? We will look at each of these in turn.

How much does SAF cost and how does that compare to jet fuel?

The cost of SAF depends on the production method and feedstock used to make it. There are three price bands:

HEFA SAF is made from used cooking oil and waste fats and accounts for all of the SAF used today. It is also the cheapest and was approximately three times the price of jet fuel before the Iran conflict – although as the price of jet fuel rose, the gap narrowed. However with waste oils and fats in limited supply, this type of SAF can not meet growing demand – building a SAF industry will require the use of other feedstocks and processes.

SAF from waste biomass – the type produced by various conversion technologies including the Nova Pangaea process – is the next most expensive, at more than four times the price of jet fuel price before the conflict. While the technology is largely tried and tested, there are few plants as yet up and running so production is an early stage.

Electro-SAF or e-SAF uses green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide and is even more costly – it would cost more than ten times the pre-conflict price of jet fuel. This type of technology is still developing so bringing it into mass production will take some time.

Typically jet fuel accounts for around 25% of the cost of a flight. The impact of SAF on ticket prices will depend on the type of SAF and the proportion used. However to get some idea, consider the following scenario involving a £100 airline ticket where SAF is three times the cost of fossil fuel.

10% SAF: Of our £100 airline ticket, £25 represents the cost of fuel. If the airline was to replace 10% of jet fuel with SAF (the level required in 2030 under the UK rules) that would add an extra £5 to the cost of the ticket, compared with using fossil fuel alone. The ticket would cost £105.

100% SAF: If the flight was to be powered entirely using SAF (though this isn’t yet allowed under current fuel standards), fuel costs would approx triple to £75, which would increase the ticket price by £50. The ticket would cost £150.

So by using SAF, ticket prices would rise, but perhaps not to the extent that the public debate might suggest.

The 3 things that haven’t been factored in

However there are a number of factors that these price comparisons fail to take into account.

Firstly, the price of jet fuel is volatile and could rise again, with demand for air travel growing and supply chain disruptions becoming ever more frequent.

Carbon taxes imposed to reflect the cost of emissions will also effectively increase the price of fossil fuels, and so over time the price gap with SAF should narrow.

Secondly, SAF production facilities are still small compared with traditional oil refineries and do not have the economies of scale or mature supply chains that have been fine-tuned over decades in the oil industry, though this will change.

Finally, at present the price of SAF is artificially high in some cases as in practice it is linked to the price of fossil fuels, even though it is from a completely different source. Tackling these last two factors will help bring down the cost of SAF and make it a more viable option .

Bringing down the cost 1: scaling production

The most powerful way to cut costs is to scale up production. Larger plants and feedstock supply chains create economies of scale and result in greater efficiency as processes improve.

Nearly every new energy technology becomes cheaper over time – solar panels, wind turbines and batteries for example – and SAF could be expected to head in a similar direction.

Building an efficient supply chain is also important. Feedstock supplies may be patchy at the start but that will change as producers become aware of this new source of revenue and coordinate collections.

For example waste biomass largely comes from pulp and sawmills at present but there is huge potential to work with farmers, set up ‘milk rounds’ to collect crop stubble and build an agricultural supply chain. The same applies to capturing waste CO2 for e-SAF.

As demand for SAF increases, the risk is that it will drive up feedstock prices. Expanding the supply and using different feedstocks will help to keep costs down so it is important we pursue all the available SAF production technologies.

Bringing down the cost 2: decoupling prices from jet fuel

Before the Iran crisis started at the end of February 2026, jet fuel was around $750/tonne while SAF was generally over $2,000/tonne – almost three times the price. Within a matter of weeks jet fuel doubled in price to more than $1,500/tonne. In theory this should have significantly narrowed the gap, but in reality something very different happened. SAF prices rose to around £2,750/tonne – just under twice the price of fossil fuel.

Most SAF is supplied on one-year contracts and the price is tied to the cost of fossil fuels because it is a formula that buyers understand. Therefore as jet fuel rises, so do SAF prices – even though the cost of producing it is unchanged. In the short term, higher prices may be a bonus for SAF producers but in the longer term it makes SAF less competitive.

As new SAF production facilities come on stream, we have the opportunity to re-think SAF pricing structures and move to a different, less volatile system to encourage wider uptake.

Amidst global instability, energy supply chains are being weaponised and fossil fuels are no longer the cheap and reliable energy source they once were. Meanwhile oil price volatility is disrupting economic stability while carbon emissions are fuelling climate change. SAF represents a genuine alternative, albeit price is a barrier.

text:
TAIPEI, Taiwan, Aug. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EVA Air today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with leading global freight forwarder AIT Worldwide Logistics (AIT) to jointly advance EVA Air's Green Transportation Program over the next two years. In the first year of the collaboration, EVA Air will provide approximately 15,000 metric tons of CO₂e in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) environmental attributes to Microsoft, helping reduce the Scope 3 emissions associated with air transportation of its cloud infrastructure equipment. Microsoft and Formosa Petrochemical Corporation (FPCC) also attended the signing ceremony, demonstrating a shared goal across the aviation, energy, logistics and technology sectors to accelerate lower-carbon air transportation.

The flights supporting this collaboration will depart from Taiwan using SAF supplied by FPCC. Produced from used cooking oil (UCO), the fuel has been certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) system for both its feedstock and production process. Compared with conventional jet fuel, it delivers approximately 80% lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. The associated SAF environmental attributes will be issued and retired through the ISCC Credit Transfer System (CTS), an internationally recognized registry for tracking sustainability attributes, enabling Microsoft to account for the resulting Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation.

In 2020, Microsoft committed to becoming carbon negative by 2030. To support this ambition, the company has continued to invest in SAF and other innovative solutions to reduce emissions across its value chain. This collaboration demonstrates how these investments and corporate demand can help accelerate SAF adoption while supporting the growth of Taiwan's domestic SAF market and a broader low-carbon aviation ecosystem.

As global demand for lower-carbon supply chains and sustainable transportation continues to grow, EVA Air has been actively expanding its SAF strategy. Since 2025, the airline has regularly incorporated SAF into flights departing from Asia, Europe and North America, while also signing a five-year SAF procurement agreement with FPCC. Through its Green Transportation Program, EVA Air helps corporate customers and freight forwarders better understand the carbon footprint of air transportation while supporting their Scope 3 decarbonization goals through SAF environmental attributes. Together with AIT, Microsoft and FPCC, EVA Air aims to establish a scalable and repeatable collaboration model that encourages broader corporate participation, expands SAF adoption and accelerates aviation's transition toward net zero.

"Achieving net-zero aviation requires collaboration across the entire value chain—from airlines and fuel suppliers to logistics providers and corporate customers," said Clay Sun, President of EVA Air. "This collaboration demonstrates that when customer demand is aligned with industry resources, it can accelerate the development of the SAF market. We look forward to working with more partners to make lower-carbon air transportation the new standard for global supply chains."

"Every year, our teams are shipping large volumes of sensitive, high-value air cargo from Taiwan. EVA Air has been the partner of choice to support our exponential growth in the region and our trust in their executive leadership is rooted in decades-long relationships," AIT's Chief Strategy Officer, Greg Weigel, said, "By demonstrating the benefits of this collaboration with Microsoft, a strategically important customer; EVA Air, one of our core carriers; and FPCC, a local SAF producer, we hope to influence the market and inspire similar collaborations between airlines, producers, forwarders and customers in the Asia-Pacific region."

The MOU was signed by Jason Liu, Chief Sustainability Officer of EVA Air, and Greg Weigel, Chief Strategy Officer of AIT Worldwide Logistics. The signing was witnessed by Shu-Ping Ho, Director General of Taiwan's Civil Aviation Administration; Eric Crowley, Commercial Section Deputy Chief at the American Institute in Taiwan; Clay Sun, President of EVA Air; Keh-Yen Lin, President of Formosa Petrochemical Corporation; Ryan Carter, Executive Vice President, Global Operations of AIT Worldwide Logistics; and Vincent Shih, General Manager of Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs for Microsoft Taiwan. Together, the four organizations represent an integrated SAF value chain spanning aviation, fuel production, logistics and corporate customers, further advancing supply chain decarbonization and the aviation industry's low-carbon transition.

EVA Air continues to strengthen its sustainability governance and disclosure practices. Since 2021, the airline has participated in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) and has been included in The Sustainability Yearbook for five consecutive years. In May 2026, EVA Air also became the only Taiwanese airline selected as a constituent of the Dow Jones Best-in-Class Emerging Markets Index (DJBIC Emerging Markets Index).

The Dow Jones Best-in-Class Indices (DJBIC) are among the world's leading sustainability benchmarks, evaluating companies across environmental, social, governance and economic dimensions based on the S&P Global CSA. This recognition reflects EVA Air's continued progress in sustainability governance and decarbonization. Looking ahead, EVA Air will continue expanding the use of SAF, improving operational efficiency, and working closely with suppliers, corporate customers and global partners to accelerate the transition toward net-zero aviation and create long-term value through sustainable growth.

About EVA Air:

A Star Alliance member, EVA Air was founded in 1989 as Taiwan's first privately owned international airline. It is an affiliated company of global container-shipping leader Evergreen Line. It flies a fleet of more than 80 Boeing and Airbus aircraft to around 60 international destinations throughout Asia, Oceania, Europe, and North America. title: Opinion: Rural America keeps blocking data centers it desperately needs - Agri-Pulse
description:
Closed factories, the opioid epidemic, and depopulation have resulted from the “elites” forcing free trade agreements on an unsuspecting and unrepresented Middle America as good jobs have moved to China.
Even Texas Governor Greg Abbott has expressed opposition to data centers.
Data centers use water for cooling, but most will use a closed system that uses very little water once the system is charged.
(And if you didn’t post all those scary stories about data centers on social media, we wouldn’t need so many data centers!)
But, when the chance to build factories for data comes to our communities, we lose our senses.
text:
The last three presidential elections have had a common theme, mainly identified with the Trump campaigns, but certainly bipartisan in nature.

The story goes something like this: globalization has been a disaster for the little guy and trade has emptied the Midwest of people, money and opportunity. Closed factories, the opioid epidemic, and depopulation have resulted from the “elites” forcing free trade agreements on an unsuspecting and unrepresented Middle America as good jobs have moved to China.

It’s a winning political message, and echoes can be heard in the campaigns and rhetoric of politicians as far apart as Sen. Bernie Sanders, President Donald Trump, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Vice President JD Vance.

So it's surprising to me that small communities all across the country are being offered a chance to see economic growth in their communities and are turning it down. According to one recent report, local opposition has blocked or delayed at least 75 U.S. data center projects in the first three months of this year, projects that had a value of over $130 billion. New York has declared a yearlong moratorium on the construction of the facilities. Even Texas Governor Greg Abbott has expressed opposition to data centers.

Opponents mostly argue on environmental grounds: Groundwater will be depleted and poisoned, forever chemicals are used, and data centers use lots of electricity — which is, if one takes the opponents at their word, fixed in supply with no chance of hiring people to build more plants that generate more electricity.

Data centers use water for cooling, but most will use a closed system that uses very little water once the system is charged. The data center proposed near my home will use municipal wastewater, which seems to be a good solution that can be applied elsewhere. This worry about water supplies in the parts of the Midwest that experienced a very wet spring strikes me as ironic. If you wanted to attend a meeting protesting the water used by data centers in Missouri this spring, you probably had to take an alternate route to the demonstration because of roads closed by flooding and the damage high water left behind.

Computers do indeed use forever chemicals, and if that causes you angst, then get rid of your iPhone, laptop, car, and everything else in your house and business that uses semiconductors, because you are part of the problem. (And if you didn’t post all those scary stories about data centers on social media, we wouldn’t need so many data centers!)

So, we’ve voted like we are in dire economic straits, demanding radical change in carefully negotiated trade agreements to hypothetically improve our economic situation by encouraging manufacturing. We’ve damaged export markets for the main products of flyover country — corn, cotton and soybeans — in order to reshore factories. But, when the chance to build factories for data comes to our communities, we lose our senses.

My Facebook feed is full of people worrying about noise, traffic and loss of farmland. Meanwhile, farmers are promised another emergency bailout because the crops produced by that disappearing farmland can’t be sold at a profit. The school my grandchildren attend has less than half the students it did when I went to school there some fifty years ago, and plenty of houses in my small town sit empty except for the occasional raccoon and, in one case, the foxes living under the collapsing front porch.

It is important to love and protect the things that make small town and rural life special, but we will lose rural places if we continue to accept decline in the rural economy. The future can be a scary place and economic growth isn’t without growing pains. But if we look around the places we live, we have to admit that the costs of certainty, which is a continuation of our present decline, are high.

Now, after decades of watching new technologies destroy our main streets and empty our small towns, we have a chance to see our populations and our economies see some benefits from new technology. We ought not turn it down.

Blake Hurst is a farmer and greenhouse grower in northwest Missouri.

description:

The Aug. 20 inauguration ceremony of the Aerobrew demonstration plant on the PSI campus brought more than 150 guests from science, politics, industry and the energy sector.
With the new demonstration plant, the emerging technology is now being operated for the first time in an industrially relevant plant design.
The inauguration of the Aerobrew demonstration plant is an important milestone on the path to more sustainable aviation.
“With our demonstration plant, we are now testing the process under real-world conditions.
text:
The Aerobrew demonstration plant, a joint sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project of the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland and Zurich-based Metafuels, was officially inaugurated Aug. 20 on the PSI campus.

Here the production of SAF is being tested and prepared for commercialization—synthetic kerosene manufactured in what PSI said is “an exceptionally efficient way.”

From water, renewable electricity and carbon dioxide from sustainable sources, high-quality, climate-neutral aviation fuel is to be created.

This is the goal of researchers at PSI in collaboration with Metafuels.

The Aug. 20 inauguration ceremony of the Aerobrew demonstration plant on the PSI campus brought more than 150 guests from science, politics, industry and the energy sector.

With the new demonstration plant, the emerging technology is now being operated for the first time in an industrially relevant plant design.

This is a novel catalytic process for producing electro SAF that PSI researchers and the Metafuels team jointly developed and patented.

The project combines scientific research with industrial development in a targeted way to transform new findings into practical applications.

“At PSI, we conduct research for society,” said PSI Director Christian Rüegg. “The energy transition is one of the major challenges we are currently facing. The inauguration of the Aerobrew demonstration plant is an important milestone on the path to more sustainable aviation. We are proud that our cutting-edge research is making a crucial contribution to this step towards industrial production.”

From green methanol to sustainable fuel

“We have successfully developed Aerobrew together with Metafuels on a laboratory scale,” said Marco Ranocchiari, a researcher at the PSI Center for Energy and Environmental Sciences, who leads PSI’s involvement in the Aerobrew project. “With our demonstration plant, we are now testing the process under real-world conditions. This will allow us to further optimize the technology and create the conditions for industrial production.”

The new plant at PSI is designed to produce 50 liters (13.2 gallons) of SAF per day.

It is the world’s first facility to combine all the production steps for synthesizing aviation fuel from methanol under one roof, according to PSI.

“International travel and global supply chains will continue to depend on air transport,” said Saurabh Kapoor, co-founder and CEO of Metafuels. “That’s why we have developed a product that can be integrated into existing airport infrastructure and used in conventional jet engines, while at the same time significantly reducing climate-damaging emissions.”

Metafuels plans to bring the first commercial plant for production of SAF using the Aerobrew technology into operation starting in 2030.

The Aerobrew process requires no fossil fuels and achieves higher selectivity—a better yield-to-revenue ratio—compared to previously used production methods for SAF, according to PSI.

The source materials are water, from which hydrogen is produced using sustainable electricity, and carbon dioxide.

The latter can in the short term be sourced from biogenic sources such as wood or plant waste, and in the long term directly from the atmosphere.

Hydrogen and carbon dioxide are processed into green methanol.
