title: The Future of High-Pressure Regulators and Valves: From Pressure Control to Operational ...
description:
As industrial organizations pursue digital transformation, operational resilience, sustainability, hydrogen adoption, and higher levels of automation, manufacturers of high-pressure regulators and valves are being challenged to deliver more than just pressure control.
Precision Pressure Control Is Becoming Increasingly Critical As industrial processes become more automated and quality requirements continue to tighten, pressure stability and control accuracy are emerging as major purchasing criteria.
As a result, pressure control accuracy is becoming as important as maximum pressure capability in many applications.
As advanced manufacturing industries continue to expand globally, demand for high-purity pressure control solutions is expected to increase significantly over the next decade.
Digitalization Is Moving into Pressure Control Industrial facilities continue to advance their digital transformation initiatives, creating new opportunities for pressure control suppliers.
text:
Beyond Pressure Ratings

For decades, the high-pressure regulator and valve market was largely defined by basic performance parameters such as pressure rating, flow capacity, and material selection. While these metrics remain important, today's industrial buyers are increasingly evaluating suppliers based on a broader set of business and operational performance indicators.

As industrial organizations pursue digital transformation, operational resilience, sustainability, hydrogen adoption, and higher levels of automation, manufacturers of high-pressure regulators and valves are being challenged to deliver more than just pressure control. End users are seeking solutions that improve reliability, reduce lifecycle costs, enhance safety, support decarbonization initiatives, and provide measurable operational value.

As ARC continues its research into the global high-pressure regulator and valve market, discussions with suppliers increasingly center on several key performance indicators (KPIs) that have emerged as the primary drivers of competitive differentiation.

Reliability Has Become the New Currency

In today's operating environment, unplanned downtime can have a significantly greater financial impact than the initial cost of a valve or regulator. Consequently, reliability has become one of the most important factors influencing supplier selection.

Manufacturers are focusing on extended service life, reduced maintenance requirements, improved sealing technologies, and enhanced product durability to help customers maximize asset availability. Whether in hydrogen fueling stations, semiconductor manufacturing facilities, chemical plants, or offshore production platforms, operators increasingly prioritize solutions that improve uptime and reduce operational risk. Suppliers that can demonstrate long-term field performance, proven installed bases, and lifecycle value are often better positioned than those competing solely on technical specifications.

Precision Pressure Control Is Becoming Increasingly Critical

As industrial processes become more automated and quality requirements continue to tighten, pressure stability and control accuracy are emerging as major purchasing criteria.

Applications such as semiconductor gas delivery, specialty gas management, laboratory operations, hydrogen fuel systems, and advanced manufacturing often require extremely stable outlet pressure regardless of fluctuations in inlet pressure or process demand. Manufacturers are investing in improved sensing technologies, advanced regulator designs, and intelligent pressure management capabilities to meet these requirements. As a result, pressure control accuracy is becoming as important as maximum pressure capability in many applications.

Safety and Leak Integrity Remain Top Priorities

The growing use of hydrogen, specialty gases, toxic chemicals, and high-value process fluids is elevating the importance of leak-tight performance.

Regulatory requirements, environmental initiatives, and corporate sustainability programs are increasing scrutiny around fugitive emissions and process safety. End users are placing greater emphasis on sealing performance, emissions compliance, material compatibility, and product testing procedures. Manufacturers that can demonstrate exceptional leak integrity, robust testing protocols, and proven performance in hazardous applications are seeing increased interest across multiple industries.

Hydrogen Is Redefining Product Development Priorities

Few market trends are generating as much attention as hydrogen. Investments in hydrogen production, storage, transportation, and fueling infrastructure are creating new requirements for pressure control technologies.

Unlike traditional industrial gases, hydrogen introduces unique challenges related to permeation, embrittlement, sealing integrity, and high-pressure operation. As a result, suppliers are accelerating investments in hydrogen-compatible materials, specialized regulator designs, and safety-focused engineering practices. Many industry participants now see hydrogen readiness as a strategic differentiator, not just another application area.

High Purity Is Expanding Beyond Semiconductor Applications

Historically associated with semiconductor manufacturing, high-purity requirements are increasingly appearing across life sciences, biotechnology, specialty chemicals, energy, and advanced industrial gas applications.

Customers are paying closer attention to particle generation, surface finish quality, contamination control, cleanroom manufacturing practices, and material traceability. These factors are becoming essential considerations during supplier selection. As advanced manufacturing industries continue to expand globally, demand for high-purity pressure control solutions is expected to increase significantly over the next decade.

Customization Continues to Create Competitive Advantage

Although many industrial customers seek standardized solutions, a growing number of applications require highly specialized products.

Hydrogen fueling systems, aerospace platforms, defense applications, subsea installations, specialty gas systems, and research facilities often present operating conditions that cannot be addressed through standard catalog offerings. Manufacturers that combine strong engineering resources with application expertise are increasingly differentiating themselves through customized solutions. In many cases, engineering support and application knowledge have become as valuable as the hardware itself.

Digitalization Is Moving into Pressure Control

Industrial facilities continue to advance their digital transformation initiatives, creating new opportunities for pressure control suppliers.

Customers are beginning to evaluate how regulators and valves can contribute to broader operational objectives such as predictive maintenance, remote asset monitoring, diagnostics, and performance optimization. While digital adoption remains in the early stages for much of the regulator market, suppliers that develop intelligent pressure management capabilities may gain a meaningful competitive advantage as industrial connectivity expands.

Lifecycle Services and Recurring Revenue

Leading suppliers are using aftermarket services, maintenance agreements, field support, and asset lifecycle management to strengthen customer relationships and create recurring revenue streams. These offerings are shifting supplier differentiation beyond equipment performance and toward long-term service value and customer support.

AI-Driven Operations and Asset Intelligence

Manufacturers are also exploring smart pressure management solutions that combine sensors, diagnostics, connectivity, and analytics. Over time, AI-enabled monitoring can help operators make better maintenance decisions, improve safety, optimize equipment utilization, and transform pressure-control assets into sources of operational intelligence.

Future Growth Opportunities by End Market

Growth opportunities are expanding across end markets that require higher levels of purity, reliability, precision, and safety. AI infrastructure, semiconductor capacity expansion, LNG, carbon capture, renewable natural gas, sustainable aviation fuel, industrial gases, aerospace and defense, nuclear energy, and advanced manufacturing are all creating new demand for advanced pressure-control solutions.

Global Support, Supply Chain Resilience, and Localization

Technical performance alone does not guarantee market success. End users increasingly value suppliers that can provide strong engineering support, rapid response times, application expertise, and global service capabilities. As manufacturing operations become increasingly globalized, customers often prefer suppliers capable of supporting projects consistently across multiple regions. This trend favors manufacturers with extensive technical resources, established distribution networks, and strong customer support organizations.

The ability to provide local expertise while maintaining global consistency is becoming an important market differentiator. Customers are increasingly evaluating suppliers based on manufacturing footprint diversity, supply chain resilience, and the ability to support regional sourcing initiatives.

The Competitive Landscape Is Evolving

Across these applications, the market is moving toward suppliers that can combine engineering depth, proven reliability, digital capabilities, and strong application support. This shift will influence how manufacturers position their portfolios, differentiate their offerings, and prioritize investment over the next decade.

The next blog in this series will take a closer look at reliability as an increasingly important performance metric for high-pressure regulators and valves and explore a critical question for suppliers and end users alike: How much is downtime worth?

text:
Here are the morning’s top stories on Tuesday, August 25, 2026

For centuries, Mexico has capitalized on growing and harvesting a plant often distilled into Tequila or Mezcal. It’s called agave and it thrives on little water and a lot of heat. Now, with a California law restricting water use on farms, Valley farmers are looking to agave as a new revenue stream on their land, and working to localize supply.

California’s highest court is weighing whether a sheriff broke the law when he seized hundreds of thousands of ballots earlier this year. The court heard oral arguments Monday.

The Trump administration has ended a long standing agreement that kept ICE out of workplaces that are being investigated by the U.S. Department of Labor.

When James Hunt planted 14 acres of agave on his secluded Merced farm last year, he thought he’d harvest it for liquor. But then he did more research on the large spiky succulent, and that dream snowballed.

“You could have spirits, agave syrup, agave inulin, biofuel, sustainable aviation fuel,” says Hunt.

He knew these ideas needed an industry in the US, so he started preaching the gospel of agave he says, to anyone who would listen.

“I was a farm manager, farm operator, and now I’m an industry advocate, trying to build out something that I think can have a lot of benefit for small farms in general,” says Hunt.

Hunt knows many growers who are testing out agave right now, but it’s not just for kicks. It’s also out of necessity, and it has to do with groundwater.

Josh Viers is a professor of civil and environmental engineering at U-C Merced. “We’re taking more water out than is going back in,” he says.

Viers is describing groundwater overdraft. That happens when groundwater gets taken out, but not replenished. It dries wells and sinks land.

So in 2014, California legislators enacted a law called the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, or SGMA to stabilize water use.

“It gave them a drawdown period over 30 years to be able to meet that sustainability target, and also to maintain some specific guardrails, you might say, about that use,” says Viers.

SGMA created local agencies to gradually limit the use of the water. That means farmers are making cuts, like watering a few inches of soil on crops like agave instead of a few feet of soil on an almond tree.

Some farmers, are more equipped than others.

Omar Ramirez is a grower in Le Grand – a community in southeast Merced County, but he also owns a Tequila line based in Mexico called Luna Yena.

“A lot of my businesses have arose from problems and there’s a common saying that if you know how to solve people’s problems, you’re always going to have work,” says Ramirez.

He lived in Mexico for a few years as a kid. In Le Grand he used to grow almonds, until profits tanked a few years ago. With SGMA in focus, he thought, ‘Why not try something familiar?’

He planted 100 acres of agave.

“As a Mexican myself, Mexican American, that light bulb lit to say, ‘Hey, you know what? I think this is a perfect way to bring both of my cultures that I really love into one location.’

He’s excited about conversations that go beyond alcohol. He might make spirits, but he’s also looking at animal feed and building materials.

He says opportunities that arise in the United States are a bit different than what are destined in Mexico.

Hunt also feels good about agave’s destiny here. Nearly all of his plants survived the winter frost, even though some have dried up tips.

It’ll be four to six years before the first batch are ready to harvest, and he’ll spend that time trying to develop the agave economy.

“Farming is a gamble,” says Hunt. “And I’m willing to go out on a limb for this because I believe in it.”

He’s lived on this land his whole life, and he’ll do whatever it takes to keep it.

Sheriff Chad Bianco of Riverside County took the ballots after last year’s statewide election on redistricting to favor Democrats.

Bianco, who’s a Republican and was then running for governor, says he was investigating voter fraud. His attorney Hertz says Bianco had a warrant and acted within the law. Specifically, that state law limits access to ballots only during prosecutions — not investigations.

But Sonni Waknin, an attorney for the plaintiffs who spoke after the hearing, says a warrant doesn’t trump California election code. Not even an elected sheriff has the power to ignore election rules and seize cast ballots outside the view of the public.

The showdown comes as California’s expansive system of vote-by-mail faces attacks not only from President Donald Trump, who has labeled mail balloting a form of cheating, but also from local election officials aligned with the president.

The court also heard a case about whether California’s Attorney General has authority to tell Bianco to stop his investigation. The court has 90 days to issue its decisions.

title: Why Are Wood Fiber Costs So High for European Pulp Producers? - ResourceWise
description:
Wood fiber is the largest component of manufacturing cash costs for many European pulp producers.
Europe's high wood fiber costs are not the result of a single market factor.
Competition for European Wood Fiber Is Increasing Pulp producers increasingly compete for wood with industries outside traditional pulp and paper markets.
What Can European Pulp Producers Do About High Fiber Costs?
Gain Deeper Insight into Global Wood Fiber Markets For pulp producers, suppliers, and investors, understanding regional fiber availability and delivered wood costs is increasingly important for evaluating competitiveness and making strategic decisions.
text:
European pulp producers face some of the highest wood fiber costs in the world due to a combination of constrained wood supply, growing competition for forest-based feedstocks, elevated log prices, changing trade flows, and regulatory pressures.

For pulp mills, these conditions have made fiber an increasingly important factor in overall production economics. In several major European pulp-producing countries, wood fiber now represents well over half of manufacturing cash costs—and in some markets, more than 70%.

Understanding what is driving those costs is essential for producers evaluating procurement strategies, mill competitiveness, and future investment.

How Much of a European Pulp Mill's Manufacturing Cost Comes from Wood Fiber?

Wood fiber is the largest component of manufacturing cash costs for many European pulp producers.

ResourceWise's WoodMarket Prices (WMP) data shows that wood fiber accounted for more than 70% of manufacturing cash costs for pulp producers in Austria and Finland in Q4 2025. Those elevated ratios continued into Q1 2026.

Across several major European markets:

Austria: Wood fiber reached approximately 73% of manufacturing cash costs in Q4 2025.

Finland: Fiber remained above 70%, despite easing from previous highs.

Sweden: Wood fiber represented approximately 64–67% of manufacturing cash costs.

Germany: Fiber's share increased from approximately 49% in early 2024 to nearly 57% by early 2026.

Source: WoodMarket Prices

These percentages vary by mill and product mix. Market pulp production, for example, is particularly exposed to wood fiber costs, while mills producing grades that use more fillers may have a lower percentage of their manufacturing costs tied directly to wood.

Temporary increases in wood availability can also influence these figures. Storm damage and other forest disturbances have periodically increased European wood supply and reduced costs, but those effects are temporary.

Learn More About WoodMarket Prices

Why Are Wood Fiber Costs So High in Europe?

Europe's high wood fiber costs are not the result of a single market factor. Instead, several structural pressures are affecting both the availability and price of pulpwood, logs, and wood chips.

1. Competition for European Wood Fiber Is Increasing

Pulp producers increasingly compete for wood with industries outside traditional pulp and paper markets.

Bioenergy, renewable fuels, engineered wood products, and biomaterials all rely on forest-based feedstocks. As these industries grow, more buyers can compete for the same underlying wood resource.

Policy can also influence this competition. Renewable-energy and fuel mandates can create demand for certain forest-derived feedstocks, allowing competing applications to support higher prices even when feedstock costs increase.

At the same time, European pulp producers have less flexibility in some traditional sourcing channels. The loss of Russian wood imports has been particularly important for Baltic and Nordic markets, including Finland, tightening regional supply and increasing dependence on other sources.

2. Log Prices Remain Well Above Historical Averages

European softwood log prices remain substantially above their 2020 levels.

ResourceWise WoodMarket Prices data shows that delivered softwood roundwood prices in Germany during 2025 were approximately 66% higher than in 2020. Finland and Sweden both recorded prices roughly 50% above 2020 levels.

There are signs of stabilization in some individual markets.

Finland's softwood pulp log prices, for example, declined approximately 17% from their Q2 2025 peak. Austria's pulp log prices also stabilized following several quarters of declines.

However, lower prices compared with recent peaks do not necessarily mean a return to historically normal costs.

Other fiber categories remain elevated. Softwood chip prices continued increasing through 2025 in Austria and Germany, while French chip prices flattened in early 2026 but remained at relatively high levels.

Longer-term wood availability is another consideration. Dry summers, high temperatures, and other forest disturbances can affect future conifer supply. Some European forest-products companies are also looking beyond their domestic markets to secure long-term access to wood resources.

3. Regulatory Changes Add Additional Pressure

European pulp and paper producers operate within an evolving regulatory environment that can affect both manufacturing costs and future wood availability.

Important policies include:

The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)

The EU Nature Restoration Regulation

The impact is not limited to direct compliance costs.

Changes to forest-management requirements can influence the amount of wood available for commercial use, while energy and emissions policies affect production economics and competition for forest-based resources.

Proposed changes to ETS benchmarks have also raised concerns about future investment. CEPI estimates that proposed benchmark reductions could reduce annual investment capacity for Europe's pulp and paper industry by approximately €1 billion, potentially affecting investment in mill modernization and decarbonization.

Restoration policies could also reduce the amount of forest available for commercial harvesting over time. If supply becomes more constrained, pulp mills may face additional competition for available wood.

How Do Energy Costs Affect Wood Fiber Prices?

Energy costs influence fiber economics before wood ever reaches a pulp mill.

Higher fuel prices increase the cost of harvesting and transporting wood, while elevated energy and chemical costs add pressure within the mill itself. This means producers can face higher costs across several stages of production simultaneously.

As a result, fiber prices need to be viewed within Europe's broader manufacturing cost environment rather than as an isolated procurement expense.

What Is the Outlook for European Wood Fiber Prices?

European wood fiber prices may fluctuate from quarter to quarter, but several structural factors suggest costs are likely to remain elevated relative to historical levels.

These include continued competition from bioenergy and biomaterials, limited growth in available wood supply, regulatory and sustainability requirements, transportation and energy costs, and uncertainty surrounding international fiber trade.

Recycling trends add another dimension to Europe's fiber balance. Policies that encourage greater use of recycled material can increase demand for recovered fiber, but recycling cannot eliminate the need for virgin fiber. Fiber is lost and degraded during repeated recycling cycles, meaning virgin wood fiber remains necessary to maintain the overall fiber system.

If paper and pulp demand strengthens, wood suppliers may respond by increasing harvest activity where possible. However, stronger demand could also intensify competition for an already constrained resource.

For European pulp producers, this means wood procurement will remain an important part of maintaining mill competitiveness.

What Can European Pulp Producers Do About High Fiber Costs?

Producers cannot control many of the structural forces affecting Europe's wood markets, but they can improve how they respond to them.

That starts with understanding how delivered wood costs vary across regions, fiber types, and competing markets. Producers can use regional pricing and supply data to benchmark procurement costs, identify changes in local fiber availability, evaluate alternative sourcing regions, and understand how their fiber position compares with competing mills.

As fiber represents a growing share of manufacturing costs, procurement intelligence becomes increasingly important to broader mill strategy.

Gain Deeper Insight into Global Wood Fiber Markets

For pulp producers, suppliers, and investors, understanding regional fiber availability and delivered wood costs is increasingly important for evaluating competitiveness and making strategic decisions.

SUBSCRIBE NOW

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is wood fiber so expensive in Europe?

Wood fiber prices are elevated because European pulp producers face constrained supply, competition from other forest-based industries, historically high log prices, reduced flexibility in international sourcing, and regulatory and energy-related pressures.

Which European countries have the highest wood fiber cost exposure?

ResourceWise data shows particularly high wood fiber shares in Austria and Finland, where fiber represented more than 70% of manufacturing cash costs in late 2025. Sweden also remained high at approximately 64–67%.

Are European wood fiber prices falling?

Some markets have eased from recent peaks, but prices generally remain elevated compared with historical levels. Finland's softwood pulp log prices, for example, declined from their Q2 2025 peak while remaining well above 2020 levels.

Why does bioenergy affect pulpwood prices?

Pulp mills and bioenergy producers can compete for overlapping forest resources. Policies supporting renewable energy and fuels can increase demand for forest-based feedstocks, adding competition within regional wood markets.

Does recycled fiber reduce demand for virgin wood fiber?

Recycling can reduce the amount of virgin fiber required for certain paper and packaging products, but it cannot replace virgin fiber entirely. Fibers degrade and are lost through successive recycling cycles, requiring new virgin fiber to enter the system.

text:
The future of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) will depend on strong partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders, according to panelists participating in a discussion during the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region. During a session titled “The Future of Flight Runs on SAF,” attendees heard how Illinois, Missouri and the broader Midwest corn belt are positioned to play a leading role in expanding domestic SAF production while creating new opportunities for agricultural producers and strengthening the aviation industry.

Moderated by Darren James, director of MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, the panel featured Jim Hedges, CEO of CoverCress, an ag-tech company developing a winter oilseed crop grown between corn and soybean seasons, and Cindy Tomei, president of the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII). The discussion focused on the current state of the SAF industry, the need for investment in production and infrastructure, and the critical role agriculture will play in meeting growing demand for lower-carbon aviation fuels.

“Illinois has emerged as a leader in the SAF space, with industry, government and research organizations collaborating to attract projects and advance the sector,” Tomei said.

She discussed how the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII) was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor's request. That event brought together stakeholders from across the aviation fuel ecosystem and highlighted the need for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)-specific testing standards, technical expertise and workforce training. She said, today, the Institute, which is headquartered in Sugar Grove, Illinois, serves as a hub for SAF education, testing and industry collaboration. It provides hands-on laboratory training in fuel testing, helps organizations understand SAF properties and blending considerations, and connects stakeholders across the global SAF supply chain.

Discussing recent progress in the SAF industry, Tomei said it has been accelerated by greater clarity around the federal 45Z tax credit and improvements in calculating carbon intensity scores, which help determine incentive eligibility.

At the same time, growing global demand, including sustainable aviation fuel mandates across the European Union and continuing challenges moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz, has increased awareness of SAF and heightened the urgency to scale production and deployment. As demand for sustainable aviation fuel continues to accelerate, Tomei said it’s increasingly important to build the infrastructure needed to move fuel from production facilities to airports. She noted that O'Hare is in one of the top 10 airports for SAF procurement worldwide.

“Speed is really of the essence, whether it is getting SAF scaled up regardless of what the feedstock is, but also having the right infrastructure to get it transported, stored and blended with jet fuel, so that it can actually be used,” Tomei said.

The panel also highlighted the important role Midwest agriculture can play in supporting SAF and other renewable fuel feedstock production. Hedges, whose company continued to hit significant milestones over the past year, noted that meeting future demand will require additional feedstocks and innovative crops that can complement existing farming operations while providing new revenue opportunities from existing acreage for producers.

“I see a huge role for Midwest agriculture,” Hedges said. “We’re crushing so many soybean acres already, but there’s no new soybean acres coming in. As all types of renewable fuels use continue to grow, we need to have supply to fulfill the demand. You have to have these new types of crops... canola, camelina, as well as CoverCress. These are crops that are planted when ground is fallow so they are truly additive to the supply of feedstock. We want everybody to be successful, because I think our biggest challenge is not meeting the demand.”

The discussion underscored how emerging feedstocks and technologies can position farmers as increasingly important participants in the future aviation fuel supply chain. Hedges explained the importance of raising awareness about the opportunity to easily grow an additional crop between corn and soybean seasons, creating a new revenue stream for farmers while improving soil health. Panelists noted that continued innovation, adoption of new crops and closer coordination throughout the production process will be essential to scaling the SAF and other renewable fuels industry.

Hedges stressed that collaboration across the fuel production ecosystem must begin early in the development process, particularly because federal Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) pathway approvals can take years. Hedges noted that CoverCress Inc just hit a major milestone with obtaining the first RFS pathway approval for CoverCress Oil, which took 2.5 years from the time the pathway was submitted.

“The earlier coordination with refiners can begin with these new crops, the better,” Hedges said. “Establish a relationship with one or more refiners. Get your pathways going as you’re doing your product development. And that way, when the product is commercially viable, it’s probably going to be around the time that you get these RFS pathway approvals.”

Panelists also discussed the rigorous testing and quality controls required for aviation fuels, the need for supportive public policies and the importance of ensuring adequate production capacity. The conversation reinforced that SAF development is not solely an aviation initiative, but one that relies on coordination among agriculture, energy, transportation and economic development stakeholders.

Looking ahead, Tomei encouraged greater collaboration among the many organizations already advancing SAF initiatives throughout Illinois. “Illinois really is a leader,” Tomei said. “There are so many good things happening in different pockets on an individual basis with SAF that, if we brought it together, we’d be an even stronger powerhouse.”

For farmers and agricultural organizations, the growth of SAF represents an opportunity to help supply a developing domestic fuel market through both established commodities and new crops, supporting farm revenue, sustainability goals and domestic energy security. “Right now, we're all kind of in that early ramp up stage, but we are planning to have hundreds of thousands of acres of these new innovative crops by the early 2030s,” Hedges said.

title: Execution, not technology, will determine whether SAF scales - SLB
description:
SAF scale-up is an execution challenge Several SAF production pathways have now reached technical maturity.
Validate constraints before choosing an SAF production pathway Selecting an SAF production pathway is arguably the most consequential strategic decision a developer faces.
HEFA accounts for the majority of commercial SAF production and is the most technologically mature of the four pathways.
PtL could become an important contributor to future SAF supply because it's less dependent on limited biological feedstocks.
Greenfield vs. asset conversion for SAF production Beyond selecting an SAF production pathway, developers must determine whether to execute the project as a greenfield development or as a conversion of an existing industrial asset.
text:
Key takeaways

Depending on the feedstock and production pathway, SAF can reduce life cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 80–90% compared with conventional jet fuel.

There's no universally optimal SAF production route. HEFA, alcohol-to-jet, Fischer-Tropsch, and power-to-liquid each bring different advantages and constraints, making local feedstock availability, infrastructure, energy availability, and policy conditions critical to technology selection.

Brownfield conversion can accelerate SAF deployment, but existing infrastructure creates value only when it’s technically suitable for the new duty and doesn’t introduce disproportionate modification costs, operating constraints, or reliability risk.

The SAF projects most likely to move forward will be those that can sustain high-quality production despite feedstock variability, utility constraints, catalyst degradation, maintenance requirements, and other real-world operating conditions.

Commercial aviation is facing one of the energy transition’s toughest decarbonization challenges. The sector’s carbon footprint accounts for roughly 2%–3% of global CO2 emissions, yet very few practical decarbonization pathways exist, especially for medium- and long-haul flights.

Commercial aircraft need fuels with exceptionally high energy density, meaning they carry substantial energy at the lowest weight possible, leaving more weight available for payload and range. Electrification and hydrogen propulsion could eventually help decarbonize aviation, especially on shorter routes. But even once electric and hydrogen aircraft are ready for production, replacing the global fleet will take decades, as today’s aircraft typically stay in service for 30 to 40 years before being retired.

Meanwhile, improvements in engines, airframes, and fleet efficiency will continue to reduce fuel consumption incrementally, which means liquid fuels will remain necessary for the foreseeable future. And with passenger air travel projected to more than double by 2050, the industry must accommodate growth while materially reducing the carbon intensity of its operations. Right now, the only viable solution is sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The SAF opportunity centers on supply rather than demand

SAF is jet fuel produced from renewable or waste-based sources—used cooking oil, waste fats, agricultural and forestry residues, municipal solid waste, alcohols, renewable hydrogen combined with captured CO2—rather than from petroleum. Developers can convert these feedstocks into usable jet fuel through several certified pathways, each relying on distinct chemical or biological processes that vary in cost, scalability, and emissions impact.

While SAF is chemically very similar to standard jet fuel and does release CO2 when burned, much of that carbon originates from recently absorbed atmospheric CO2 or from waste streams, rather than from newly extracted fossil resources. That distinction—recycled carbon versus newly extracted carbon—is what reduces its net carbon footprint. Depending on the specific pathway and feedstock, SAF life cycle greenhouse gas emissions can be 80%–90% lower than fossil-based jet fuel.

Another advantage of SAF is that airlines don’t have to modify existing aircraft engines to use it. Most commercial aircraft today are approved to use a fifty-fifty SAF blend with standard jet fuel. Engine and aircraft makers operate within blending limits set by specific production pathways and technical standards, though they’re working toward 100% SAF certification. Airbus, for instance, has pledged that its commercial aircraft will be certified for 100% SAF by 2030. Airports offering SAF can also use existing fuel storage, handling, and distribution systems with little or no modifications. San Francisco International Airport is a good example; it was the first airport to receive SAF via the same pipeline originally built for conventional jet fuel.

Recent policy developments and market activity also reflect SAF's potential, with many governments now introducing blending mandates, tax incentives, subsidies, and other financial support mechanisms to accelerate adoption. The European Union’s (EU) ReFuelEU aviation regulation is among the best-known. From 2025, it’s called for a minimum SAF share of 2% at EU airports, rising to 70% by 2050.

Airlines are also expanding long-term offtake commitments, or contracts to purchase a set volume of fuel over multiple years. Air France-KLM agreed to purchase up to 1.5 million tons of SAF through 2035. Similarly, International Airlines Group contracted for 785,000 tons over 14 years to support its five European airlines, including British Airways, Iberia, and Aer Lingus.

These measures, combined with the industry’s own ambition to decarbonize, are spurring substantial demand growth. What remains uncertain is whether SAF producers can create enough supply at a price the market can sustain.

SAF scale-up is an execution challenge

Several SAF production pathways have now reached technical maturity. Hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), alcohol-to-jet (AtJ), Fischer-Tropsch (FT), and power-to-liquid (PtL) can all produce fuels suitable for flight, although they differ in feedstock requirements, process configurations, and potential for large-scale development.

Choosing a pathway is only the first decision. Developers must also determine how well that pathway integrates with a facility’s feedstock supply, logistics, utilities, hydrogen, supporting infrastructure, and plant operations. Constraints or underperformance in any one of those areas can materially affect a project's bankability—its ability to secure financing and achieve final investment decision (FID).

For example, early-stage project models often assume steady feedstock volumes, predictable quality, and secure long-term supply agreements. In reality, feedstock availability fluctuates considerably, while quality variations introduce operational challenges that directly affect plant performance.

Developers also tend to underestimate the impact of contaminants. Metals, phosphorus, water content, and solids can shorten catalyst life, increase maintenance requirements, reduce yields, and disrupt downstream operations. Facilities that lack sufficient pretreatment investment may be exposed to operational instability that can’t be solved further downstream.

Infrastructure dependencies create additional obstacles. Hydrogen availability, utilities access, transportation networks, storage capacity, and product distribution channels all influence project viability. Those factors are often identified late in development, when changes become expensive and difficult to implement.

Financing adds another layer of complexity. Investors increasingly scrutinize feedstock security, operational flexibility, technology integration, and project execution risks. A technically sound concept may struggle to achieve FID if assumptions around supply chains, logistics, or plant integration are uncertain.

Overall, economics continues to be one of the biggest barriers to scaling SAF. While airlines will need increasing volumes to meet regulatory requirements and decarbonization commitments, SAF continues to command a substantial premium over conventional jet fuel. This price differential limits voluntary uptake beyond mandated blending requirements.

Over the next few years, the pace of industry growth will closely tie to policy support mechanisms, including tax incentives, subsidies, contracts for difference, and other funding schemes that bridge the gap between production costs and market demand. Until production scales enough to narrow the cost gap with conventional aviation fuel, or new policy frameworks emerge to support demand, commercial viability will remain every bit as important as technological readiness.

Validate constraints before choosing an SAF production pathway

Selecting an SAF production pathway is arguably the most consequential strategic decision a developer faces. As with any industry, and particularly in the energy sector, there's a natural tendency to choose the most mature technology and then build the project around it. But we argue the reverse is a lower-risk approach.

In practice, that means validating local constraints on feedstocks, infrastructure, utilities, markets, and policy in a given region, and then determining which pathway best aligns with those conditions.

Today, that means choosing among four dominant routes:

Hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids—Mature but feedstock constrained. HEFA accounts for the majority of commercial SAF production and is the most technologically mature of the four pathways. Its primary constraint is feedstock. Facilities depend on access to suitable lipid-based materials, such as used cooking oil and waste fats. Where those resources are abundant and competitively priced, HEFA provides an attractive route to market. But maturity alone can’t overcome poor feedstock economics where supply is constrained or competition is intense.

Alcohol-to-jet—Opportunity but market-dependent. AtJ offers another route to expanding SAF supply, particularly in regions with established ethanol or other alcohol production. Existing agricultural, logistics, and fuel infrastructure can strengthen the business case, but project economics are highly dependent on feedstock cost, availability, and carbon intensity, as well as regional market conditions. As with HEFA, the technology alone doesn’t determine success—the system around it does.

Fischer-Tropsch—Flexible but more complex. FT pathways can access a wider range of resources, including biomass, waste streams, and municipal solid waste. That broader feedstock base can diversify feedstock supply and potentially improve long-term resilience. The trade-off is complexity. Gasification, synthesis gas conditioning, FT conversion, upgrading, and supporting utilities create a more integrated process with additional interfaces that developers must engineer and operations teams must manage effectively.

Power-to-liquid—Promising but infrastructure-heavy. PtL could become an important contributor to future SAF supply because it's less dependent on limited biological feedstocks. Instead, it combines renewable hydrogen with a carbon source to produce synthetic hydrocarbons. PtL’s primary hurdles are infrastructure requirements, which can be prohibitive. Access to abundant low-cost renewable electricity, electrolyzer capacity, reliable CO2 supply, water, and supporting grid infrastructure will typically determine project viability before considering the fuel synthesis process itself.

Greenfield vs. asset conversion for SAF production

Beyond selecting an SAF production pathway, developers must determine whether to execute the project as a greenfield development or as a conversion of an existing industrial asset. That decision has significant implications for process design, capital intensity, integration complexity, and long-term operability.

Greenfield projects provide the greatest degree of design freedom. Developers can engineer them as an integrated system around the specific requirements of the selected SAF pathway:

feedstock receiving and pretreatment

conversion units

hydrogen production and distribution

utilities

storage

offsites

product logistics

That freedom can simplify process integration and improve overall plant efficiency, but it typically entails higher capital requirements, a broader infrastructure scope, and longer permitting and execution schedules.

Brownfield conversions offer a different value proposition by leveraging existing processing equipment, utility systems, tankage, logistics infrastructure, site services, and workforce capabilities. Matching an existing asset to new process requirements can reduce capital scope, shorten development timelines, and lower execution risk—which is why we see a significant share of early SAF capacity developed through refinery conversions, coprocessing configurations, and projects integrated with existing renewable fuels infrastructure.

The challenge is that reuse potential is highly site-specific and can be overstated during early-stage development. Take a refinery’s existing hydrotreater, for example. On paper, it can appear ready for HEFA conversion, but its metallurgy—built for crude-derived feedstocks—may not be rated for the corrosivity of used cooking oil or waste fats, and retrofitting it can be costly. Systems that appear suitable for reuse at the conceptual stage may require substantial revamping, derating, or complete replacement once detailed engineering confirms actual operating conditions and integration requirements.

In all cases, developers need rigorous techno-economic assessments to determine which assets can be viably repurposed, where modifications are required, and whether the overall conversion project can deliver a competitive business case.

Success with SAF depends on a systems-level perspective

Like most downstream facilities, an SAF plant isn't simply a collection of independent technology packages. It's a tightly connected production system, with each part of the process closely dependent on those that lie upstream of it. Feedstock handling and pretreatment must deliver a consistent input to the conversion process. What comes out of conversion, in turn, must align with downstream upgrading and separation, while hydrogen supply keeps pace with process demand.

At the same time, developers must size and coordinate supporting utility and logistics systems to maintain stable operation across a range of feedstocks and operating conditions.

Problems, when they emerge, typically appear at the interfaces rather than within individual pieces of equipment, which explains why rated plant capacity can be a misleading measure of project attractiveness. Plants that achieve consistent uptime and stable performance frequently outperform facilities chasing aggressive production targets that real operating conditions can’t support. Likewise, investments in pretreatment, separation technologies, and operational flexibility often generate greater long-term value than attempts to minimize upfront capital costs.

Few, if any, organizations have expertise across every part of the SAF production system. Licensing the technology, supplying feedstock, engineering the plant, and running it day-to-day typically involves four different parties with four different contracts. Each may be highly capable within its own scope, but fragmented responsibility can create gaps at the interfaces between those scopes. That’s where integration capability becomes particularly valuable.

cargo-partner’s SMF program enables customers to reduce emissions associated with their ocean freight shipments by using Hapag-Lloyd’s “Ship Green” solution. Between January and June, these reductions were achieved through the use of 259.46 t of waste- and residue-based biofuel in Hapag-Lloyd’s fleet.

Helping customers meet sustainability targets

Erich Schatz, Chief Operating Officer Overseas of cargo-partner, stated: “By offering certified lower-emission transport solutions, we help our customers make measurable progress toward their sustainability targets. The results achieved in the first half of 2026 demonstrate the growing demand for practical and credible solutions to reduce emissions in global supply chains.”

Danny Smolders, Managing Director, Global Sales at Hapag-Lloyd, added: “Our collaboration with cargo-partner shows how sustainable marine fuels can deliver tangible results today. Through Ship Green, we are helping customers reduce emissions and advance their sustainability goals.”

Transparent reporting and sourcing

The reports show that cargo-partner achieved CO₂e reductions of 290.58 t in the first quarter and 520.42 t in the second quarter of 2026 through its sustainable marine fuel program, totaling 811 t for the first half of the year. This is comparable to the emissions from an average passenger car driving more than 3.2 million kilometers – approximately 80 times around the Earth. The reductions were calculated on a Well-to-Wake basis, compared with emissions that would have resulted from using standard fossil fuels.

The biofuels were sourced from sustainable supply chains complying with the EU Renewable Energy Directive II (EU RED-II). The process is based on the Hapag-Lloyd Ship Green Process Report 2025 and has undergone limited independent assurance in accordance with ISAE 3000 (Revised).

Comprehensive sustainability strategy

The initiative forms part of cargo-partner’s broader sustainability approach, based on the principles Measure – Optimize – Reduce. Through its SPOT platform, the company provides shipment-level greenhouse-gas emissions data and supports customers in identifying more efficient routes, improving capacity utilization, and selecting lower-emission transport options.

In addition to Sustainable Marine Fuel, cargo-partner offers further certified insetting solutions, including Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), rail transport, electric trucks, and Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO). The company is also expanding the use of renewable energy at its facilities and strengthening environmental management standards across its global network.

cargo-partner’s sustainability efforts were recognized once again in 2026 with an EcoVadis Silver Medal. Looking ahead, cargo-partner remains committed to turning sustainability objectives into measurable action and helping customers reduce the environmental impact of their supply chains and their global CO₂e footprint.

text:
Sunoil and BFT have converted the Birjo II barge to operate entirely on 100% biodiesel, in a move aimed at cutting emissions from inland waterway transport, biofuels international reported.

Owned by DK Shipping, the Birjo II transports biofuels on Dutch inland waterways. It mainly carries biodiesel from Sunoil’s production facility in Kampen to storage sites and also makes direct deliveries to customers.

The conversion allows the vessel to use B100 instead of fossil fuel without replacing its engine. Sunoil said this can reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 90% while allowing the barge to continue normal operations.

The companies said the Birjo II is among the first barges in the world capable of operating fully on 100% biodiesel.

The project is part of the long-term cooperation between Sunoil and BFT and is intended to demonstrate that existing inland vessels can be converted to use renewable fuels.

The barge can now be fuelled directly at Sunoil’s Kampen facility, linking fuel production, transport and final use in a single renewable fuel chain.

“What makes this project especially valuable for Sunoil is that Birjo II now operates on our own biodiesel while transporting renewable fuels between our locations and customers,” said Jeroen Hovius, chief commercial officer at Sunoil.

He said the partnership with BFT was focused on practical measures to make inland shipping more sustainable and could support the conversion of more barges to B100 across Europe.

Edwardsville: The future of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) will depend on strong partnerships among farmers, fuel producers, the aviation industry and government leaders, according to panelists participating in a discussion during the 2026 Global Aerospace Summit in the St. Louis region. During a session titled “The Future of Flight Runs on SAF,” attendees heard how Illinois, Missouri and the broader Midwest corn belt are positioned to play a leading role in expanding domestic SAF production while creating new opportunities for agricultural producers and strengthening the aviation industry, according to a press release.

Moderated by Darren James, director of MidAmerica St. Louis Airport, the panel featured Jim Hedges, CEO of CoverCress, an ag-tech company developing a winter oilseed crop grown between corn and soybean seasons, and Cindy Tomei, president of the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII). The discussion focused on the current state of the SAF industry, the need for investment in production and infrastructure, and the critical role agriculture will play in meeting growing demand for lower-carbon aviation fuels.

“Illinois has emerged as a leader in the SAF space, with industry, government and research organizations collaborating to attract projects and advance the sector,” Tomei said.

She discussed how the Sustainable Aviation Fuels Institute (SAFII) was established in Illinois two years ago following a state-led SAF summit convened at the governor’s request. That event brought together stakeholders from across the aviation fuel ecosystem and highlighted the need for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)-specific testing standards, technical expertise and workforce training. She said, today, the Institute, which is headquartered in Sugar Grove, Illinois, serves as a hub for SAF education, testing and industry collaboration. It provides hands-on laboratory training in fuel testing, helps organizations understand SAF properties and blending considerations, and connects stakeholders across the global SAF supply chain.

Discussing recent progress in the SAF industry, Tomei said it has been accelerated by greater clarity around the federal 45Z tax credit and improvements in calculating carbon intensity scores, which help determine incentive eligibility.

At the same time, growing global demand, including sustainable aviation fuel mandates across the European Union and continuing challenges moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz, has increased awareness of SAF and heightened the urgency to scale production and deployment. As demand for sustainable aviation fuel continues to accelerate, Tomei said it’s increasingly important to build the infrastructure needed to move fuel from production facilities to airports. She noted that O’Hare is in one of the top 10 airports for SAF procurement worldwide.

“Speed is really of the essence, whether it is getting SAF scaled up regardless of what the feedstock is, but also having the right infrastructure to get it transported, stored and blended with jet fuel, so that it can actually be used,” Tomei said.

The panel also highlighted the important role Midwest agriculture can play in supporting SAF and other renewable fuel feedstock production. Hedges, whose company continued to hit significant milestones over the past year, noted that meeting future demand will require additional feedstocks and innovative crops that can complement existing farming operations while providing new revenue opportunities from existing acreage for producers.

“I see a huge role for Midwest agriculture,” Hedges said. “We’re crushing so many soybean acres already, but there’s no new soybean acres coming in. As all types of renewable fuels use continue to grow, we need to have supply to fulfill the demand. You have to have these new types of crops… canola, camelina, as well as CoverCress. These are crops that are planted when ground is fallow so they are truly additive to the supply of feedstock. We want everybody to be successful, because I think our biggest challenge is not meeting the demand.”

The discussion underscored how emerging feedstocks and technologies can position farmers as increasingly important participants in the future aviation fuel supply chain. Hedges explained the importance of raising awareness about the opportunity to easily grow an additional crop between corn and soybean seasons, creating a new revenue stream for farmers while improving soil health. Panelists noted that continued innovation, adoption of new crops and closer coordination throughout the production process will be essential to scaling the SAF and other renewable fuels industry.

Hedges stressed that collaboration across the fuel production ecosystem must begin early in the development process, particularly because federal Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) pathway approvals can take years. Hedges noted that CoverCress Inc just hit a major milestone with obtaining the first RFS pathway approval for CoverCress Oil, which took 2.5 years from the time the pathway was submitted.

“The earlier coordination with refiners can begin with these new crops, the better,” Hedges said. “Establish a relationship with one or more refiners. Get your pathways going as you’re doing your product development. And that way, when the product is commercially viable, it’s probably going to be around the time that you get these RFS pathway approvals.”

Panelists also discussed the rigorous testing and quality controls required for aviation fuels, the need for supportive public policies and the importance of ensuring adequate production capacity. The conversation reinforced that SAF development is not solely an aviation initiative, but one that relies on coordination among agriculture, energy, transportation and economic development stakeholders.

Looking ahead, Tomei encouraged greater collaboration among the many organizations already advancing SAF initiatives throughout Illinois. “Illinois really is a leader,” Tomei said. “There are so many good things happening in different pockets on an individual basis with SAF that, if we brought it together, we’d be an even stronger powerhouse.”

For farmers and agricultural organizations, the growth of SAF represents an opportunity to help supply a developing domestic fuel market through both established commodities and new crops, supporting farm revenue, sustainability goals and domestic energy security. “Right now, we’re all kind of in that early ramp up stage, but we are planning to have hundreds of thousands of acres of these new innovative crops by the early 2030s,” Hedges said.

The second annual Global Aerospace Summit brought together aerospace manufacturers, suppliers and leaders in military, cargo movement, transportation, economic development and other sectors for a two-day program focused on advancing innovation and strengthening the industry’s future. The event was presented by the Leadership Council Southwestern Illinois, Madison County and St. Clair County, Illinois, and Bi-State Development’s St. Louis Regional Freightway.

text:

By Chen Aizhu

SINGAPORE, Aug 25 (Reuters) – Hou Qijun has set out to transform Sinopec, the world’s largest refiner, as it faces dwindling fuel demand, overcapacity in petrochemicals and the world’s worst oil crisis, when he could be coasting into retirement like other Chinese state executives.

Appointed as Sinopec chairman a year ago, Hou launched an overhaul to give greater authority to business units ​that he revamped into four profit centres: oil, gas and new energy, refining and chemicals, finance and strategic new business, and a segment ‌combining global trading with Sinopec’s vast marketing teams for fuel, natural gas and chemicals.

He outlined his thinking in unusually blunt language for a state enterprise chief in a government magazine in July.

“The biggest hurdles for such a self-revolutionary transformation lie not on technology, resources or markets, but the system and institutional inertia,” Hou said in the July issue of a publication by China’s powerful State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC).

“As the company grows in scale, its ability to respond to market changes becomes inadequate, and the ‘big company syndrome’ remains to be overcome,” he said.

Sinopec referred ‌to the ​SASAC publication when Reuters sought comment from Hou about his plans to revive the company.

Its fuel sales have ⁠dropped to 2017 levels and it faces an “uphill ⁠battle” to maintain domestic market share, the SASAC magazine said.

An executive with a Chinese institutional investor that owns shares in Sinopec said Hou, at 60, appears to be on a mission to “salvage Sinopec, which has been fighting for survival in a tight spot.”

“Hou is among the few SOE executives who, despite being close to retirement age, is spirited and wants to make some changes,” said the investor, declining to be named due to company policy.

Executives ​at Chinese state firms typically retire at 63.

TOUGH TIMES

On Sunday, Sinopec reported a 19% rise in net profit for the first half of 2026, despite its heavy exposure to oil supply disruptions due to the Iran war and government curbs on passing higher oil prices on to consumers.

Sinopec sold around 3.6 million barrels ⁠per day of gasoline and diesel last year according to company data, mostly at home, ⁠a scale that has become a liability as demand for transport fuels declines with widening vehicle electrification.

“Gasoline was made for ​cars, yet half of new cars no longer need fuel … Under these circumstances, how can producing more gasoline and diesel continue to generate revenue?” Hou said at an ​earnings briefing in Hong Kong on Monday.

“We need to produce more chemical materials instead. In the long run, upstream oil and ‌gas will likewise be replaced by new energy, from high-carbon, to low-carbon, to zero-carbon. Therefore, we must prepare early and develop new energy.”

Sinopec plans to allocate about 20% of its capital spending, or more than 30 billion yuan ($4.46 billion) a year, on new energy and new materials over 2026 to 2030, he said.

In the SASAC report, Hou targeted completion of more than 30 projects by 2030, including growing reserves, producing shale oil, developing sustainable aviation fuel and cutting refining costs.

Such investments focus on “converting ⁠technology into productivity”, he said, calling for “expediting execution”.

The company’s shift to higher-value petrochemicals faces fierce competition from rivals such as local government-backed Wanhua Chemical and privately-led Satellite Chemical as well as overcapacity in ethylene, a key building block in plastics and fiber.

PLAN 2030

In shale, Sinopec is set to start commercial development at the Jiyang ⁠trough, part of its flagship Shengli oilfield, where conventionally-accessible reserves ‌are fast depleting. Hou told reporters in March he was the project’s commander-in-chief.

As a geologist, he built his career ⁠at China’s flagship Daqing oilfield and was general manager of Asia’s largest oil and gas producer, China National Petroleum ​Corp (CNPC), before moving ‌to Sinopec in June 2025.

The Shandong native established his restructuring credentials combining the pipeline assets of China’s three ​oil majors into ⁠a new state firm, PipeChina, which he ran from 2019 to 2021.

A company official described Hou as a “decisive, quick-in-action” workaholic who can speak “off-script for half an hour with conviction and logic”.

With his experience at CNPC and PipeChina, he has a good grasp of the whole energy value chain and could capitalise on government backing for commercially challenging investments such as hydrogen and carbon capture, said Michal Meidan, director of the China program at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

“The question is how will Sinopec (and its peers) compete with the non-state actors in the new energy space,” she said.

($1 = 6.7238 Chinese yuan renminbi)

(Reporting by Chen Aizhu; Additional reporting by Sam Li and Alison Lui; ​Editing by Tony Munroe and Sonali Paul)

"Hou is among the few SOE executives who, despite being close to retirement age, is spirited and wants to make some changes," said the investor, declining to be named due to company policy.

Executives at Chinese State firms typically retire at 63.

TOUGH TIMES

On Sunday, Sinopec reported a 19% rise in net profit for the first half of 2026, despite its heavy exposure to oil supply disruptions due to the Iran war and government curbs on passing higher oil prices on to consumers.

Sinopec sold around 3.6-million barrels per day of gasoline and diesel last year according to company data, mostly at home, a scale that has become a liability as demand for transport fuels declines with widening vehicle electrification.

"Gasoline was made for cars, yet half of new cars no longer need fuel ... Under these circumstances, how can producing more gasoline and diesel continue to generate revenue?" Hou said at an earnings briefing in Hong Kong on Monday.

"We need to produce more chemical materials instead. In the long run, upstream oil and gas will likewise be replaced by new energy, from high-carbon, to low-carbon, to zero-carbon. Therefore, we must prepare early and develop new energy."

Sinopec plans to allocate about 20% of its capital spending, or more than 30-billion yuan ($4.46-billion) a year, on new energy and new materials over 2026 to 2030, he said.

In the SASAC report, Hou targeted completion of more than 30 projects by 2030, including growing reserves, producing shale oil, developing sustainable aviation fuel and cutting refining costs.

Such investments focus on "converting technology into productivity", he said, calling for "expediting execution".

The company's shift to higher-value petrochemicals faces fierce competition from rivals such as local government-backed Wanhua Chemical and privately-led Satellite Chemical as well as overcapacity in ethylene, a key building block in plastics and fiber.

PLAN 2030

In shale, Sinopec is set to start commercial development at the Jiyang trough, part of its flagship Shengli oilfield, where conventionally-accessible reserves are fast depleting. Hou told reporters in March he was the project's commander-in-chief.

As a geologist, he built his career at China's flagship Daqing oilfield and was general manager of Asia's largest oil and gas producer, China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC), before moving to Sinopec in June 2025.

The Shandong native established his restructuring credentials combining the pipeline assets of China's three oil majors into a new State firm, PipeChina, which he ran from 2019 to 2021.

A company official described Hou as a "decisive, quick-in-action" workaholic who can speak "off-script for half an hour with conviction and logic".

With his experience at CNPC and PipeChina, he has a good grasp of the whole energy value chain and could capitalise on government backing for commercially challenging investments such as hydrogen and carbon capture, said Michal Meiden, director of the China program at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

"The question is how will Sinopec (and its peers) compete with the non-State actors in the new energy space," she said.

title: An integrated CNS solution for low-altitude aircraft operations - Innovation News Network
description:
The ANTENNAE project is exploring a 3GPP-compliant integrated CNS solution for Innovative Air Mobility (IAM), including piloted and U-space operations at low altitude.
You may think: can we use the same hardware and technologies used for manned aircraft to support CNS services for unmanned aircraft?
ANTENNAE’s approach towards integrated CNS for low-altitude aviation There is a pressing need for a new CNS solution for low-altitude IAM operations.
Therefore, the new CNS solution for unmanned aircraft must be capable of handling hundreds of aircraft simultaneously to ensure the safety of aircraft, infrastructure, and the public.
How can CNS services be delivered to aircraft when they fly beyond the coverage of terrestrial networks?
text:
The ANTENNAE project is developing an innovative integrated CNS solution for aircraft operating at low altitude

The ANTENNAE project explores the applicability of 3GPP 5G and next-generation hybrid terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks for providing Communication, Navigation, and Surveillance (CNS) services to aircraft operating at low altitude. The ANTENNAE project is exploring a 3GPP-compliant integrated CNS solution for Innovative Air Mobility (IAM), including piloted and U-space operations at low altitude. The solution will support safe low-altitude air traffic by providing reliable, affordable communication, navigation, and surveillance services to ensure strict adherence to flight paths, real-time traffic separation, and robust airspace boundary protection.

Why legacy CNS is not enough for low-altitude aviation

CNS is designed to provide three separate services: “C” – Communication, “N” – Navigation, and “S” – Surveillance. However, all three services rely on one common thing: wireless network infrastructure and its coverage. We need radio signals for the timely exchange of information between aircraft, between aircraft and the ground, and sometimes between ground systems. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals help aircraft safely navigate designated routes and flight paths. Similarly, radio signals carrying critical information, including an aircraft’s location, altitude, ground speed, and surveillance data, are vital for aircraft tracking and maintaining safe separation between aircraft.

Legacy CNS is designed for manned aircraft and uses a combination of hardware, with each system dedicated to a specific service. For example, ADS-B, VDL/ACARS, transponders (Mode A/C/S), VOR/ILS receivers, and SATCOM all use different hardware and handle different services. You may think: can we use the same hardware and technologies used for manned aircraft to support CNS services for unmanned aircraft? The short answer is no, and here are the reasons.

First, legacy CNS coverage is optimised for airports and high-altitude air corridors. Due to ground structures that cause blockages, legacy CNS faces coverage problems at low altitudes. One may consider solving this challenge by expanding coverage to low altitudes through large-scale deployment of CNS infrastructure, but this would entail significant capital and operational costs. Second, it will be challenging for small, unmanned aircraft to carry fragmented CNS hardware systems and sufficient battery capacity to power multiple devices. Third, even if we successfully solve the first two problems today, how about the future? Legacy CNS systems may not have sufficient bandwidth to accommodate thousands of small automated aircraft operating at low altitudes.

ANTENNAE’s approach towards integrated CNS for low-altitude aviation

There is a pressing need for a new CNS solution for low-altitude IAM operations. We need a solution that does not require multiple onboard hardware devices, consumes less energy, and can run on small batteries. We need a solution that is highly spectrum-efficient to accommodate hundreds to thousands of aircraft flying in our urban skies at low altitudes. Let us consider a practical example. In the future, unmanned aircraft, also called drones, will be delivering food and groceries. Imagine a lunchtime period when hundreds of people working from home may order food online, and hundreds of drones may have to share the airspace as well as available radio network resources for CNS services. Therefore, the new CNS solution for unmanned aircraft must be capable of handling hundreds of aircraft simultaneously to ensure the safety of aircraft, infrastructure, and the public.

This is where the ANTENNAE project’s vision and its integrated CNS (ICNS) concept come into play. ANTENNAE project envisions delivering the “C”, “N”, and “S” services through the same technology, hardware, and frequency spectrum. This means that ICNS will eliminate the need for multiple onboard hardware systems, make efficient use of spectrum, and allow “C”, “N”, and “S” services to support and complement each other.

Today, 4G and 5G networks provide extensive coverage worldwide, with 4G covering around 90% of the global population. These cellular networks have a native ability to support massive numbers of users simultaneously. You may wonder: can these same terrestrial networks support CNS services at low altitude? According to ANTENNAE project’s exploratory research, the answer is yes, but there are some limitations.

The ANTENNAE project explores the applicability of 3GPP telecommunications standards for delivering ICNS services at low altitude to support both piloted and U-space operations. It is worth emphasising that coverage of 5G terrestrial networks is optimised to serve users located on the ground, on streets, and in buildings. Researchers outside the ANTENNAE consortium have conducted real-world experimental measurements which confirmed the feasibility of connecting an unmanned aircraft to a 5G base station. However, there is a noticeable performance degradation as aircraft altitude increases because these base stations use down-tilted antennas.

This presents a considerable design challenge for future networks. How can CNS services be delivered to aircraft when they fly beyond the coverage of terrestrial networks? This is where non-terrestrial networks, especially direct-to-device connectivity, become important. To complement the poor coverage above terrestrial base stations, the ANTENNAE solution uses 3GPP hybrid terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks to ensure continuous coverage for CNS services. In particular, the ANTENNAE solution uses direct-to-device connectivity, which allows a transceiver on the aircraft to automatically switch to a satellite connection when the aircraft moves outside terrestrial network coverage without interrupting CNS services.
