title: US Renewable Diesel Prices Are Surging, Questioning RIN Supply - ResourceWise
description:
The US renewable diesel market is getting a powerful lift from an increasingly tight diesel market.
Tight Diesel Supplies Are Supporting Renewable Diesel The ongoing US-Iran standoff continues to weigh on global crude oil and refined-product supply expectations.
As diesel prices strengthened, heating oil values increased faster than renewable diesel feedstock costs.
In other words, high diesel prices are currently doing some of the economic work that higher RIN prices might otherwise need to do.
Strong Margins Do Not Guarantee Domestic RIN Supply High diesel prices are creating the margin environment needed to support strong utilization across US renewable diesel and biodiesel plants.
text:
The US renewable diesel market is getting a powerful lift from an increasingly tight diesel market. But stronger prices do not necessarily mean more renewable fuel will stay in the United States.

That distinction is becoming increasingly important as renewable diesel producers weigh domestic demand against attractive export opportunities, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production, and shifting incentive structures.

At the center of the market right now is a simple question:

Will enough biomass-based diesel remain in the domestic market to generate the RINs needed to meet US mandates?

Tight Diesel Supplies Are Supporting Renewable Diesel

The ongoing US-Iran standoff continues to weigh on global crude oil and refined-product supply expectations. Without a lasting resolution, crude and diesel prices have continued to climb.

That is providing substantial support to biomass-based diesel prices, which remain near record highs. And the timing is significant.

According to a Prima CarbonZero analyst report, US renewable diesel production has already experienced downtime in August. This is reflected in relatively subdued feedstock buying and grease and soybean oil prices that remain below their recent peaks. At the same time, conventional diesel demand is beginning to strengthen ahead of the September harvest.

The overall result is a tighter diesel market. Ultra-low sulfur diesel inventories entered August 13.6% below the five-year average. Meanwhile, concerns surrounding refinery output in both the United States and international markets have helped push diesel crack spreads to record highs.

Unless the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz changes materially, those conditions could continue supporting diesel prices into the fourth quarter. And that support is flowing directly into renewable diesel economics.

Heating Oil Has Become a Bigger Part of the Revenue Story

One of the most important changes in renewable diesel economics has occurred within the producer revenue stack.

Since early July, heating oil has become the largest component of renewable diesel revenue. Earlier in the year, D4 RIN prices played the more prominent role as optimism grew that the United States and Iran might reach an agreement.

That optimism faded as the Strait of Hormuz remained constrained.

As diesel prices strengthened, heating oil values increased faster than renewable diesel feedstock costs. That has reduced some of the pressure on D4 RIN prices to climb high enough to bring more marginal renewable diesel and biodiesel production online.

In other words, high diesel prices are currently doing some of the economic work that higher RIN prices might otherwise need to do.

That helps maintain strong production margins across the US biomass-based diesel sector. But it does not eliminate the market's underlying supply question.

Strong Margins Do Not Guarantee Domestic RIN Supply

High diesel prices are creating the margin environment needed to support strong utilization across US renewable diesel and biodiesel plants.

Rising Low Carbon Fuel Standard prices are adding another layer of support. For some producers, LCFS (Low Carbon Fuel Standard) value is now providing a stronger incentive than the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit to maximize sales into the West Coast market.

Transportation economics are also becoming more favorable. The latest 90-day extension of the Jones Act waiver has improved the economics of moving fuel by sea from the Gulf Coast to other US markets.

The Jones Act generally requires cargo transported between US ports to be carried on US-built, US-owned vessels qualified for coastwise trade. The temporary waiver allows covered cargo to move on foreign-flagged vessels. This expands available shipping capacity and potentially reduces transportation constraints.

For renewable diesel producers, that could make it more attractive to move Gulf Coast barrels to higher-value domestic markets, including the West Coast.

Taken together, these factors should encourage production. Yet production volume alone does not determine how many RINs ultimately reach the US market.

The bigger question is where those barrels go.

Exports Are Competing With Domestic Compliance Demand

Some US renewable diesel production capacity is expected to remain focused on export markets, where producers may be able to capture stronger margins.

That opportunity is partly supported by feedstock economics.

Renewable diesel produced for export can potentially benefit from feedstocks priced well below supplies qualifying under US-Mexico-Canada Agreement-related incentive structures. When those economics are sufficiently attractive, exporting finished product can compete directly with selling fuel domestically and generating RINs.

Recent declines in demand for imported feedstocks thought to be destined for export-oriented renewable diesel production suggest that activity may have slowed. But the underlying incentive remains.

And that creates an important tension for the US market. The country may have substantial renewable diesel production capacity, but not all of it necessarily contributes to domestic RIN generation.

SAF Adds Another Layer of Competition

Sustainable aviation fuel could further complicate that equation.

Renewable diesel producers increasingly have multiple pathways for monetizing their production capacity. Depending on plant configuration and market economics, some capacity can be redirected toward SAF.

That opens additional revenue opportunities through both physical SAF sales and SAF-related credits. For producers, that flexibility can be valuable.

For the RIN market, however, it introduces another potential source of supply competition.

Every gallon of production capacity directed toward an alternative market is capacity that may not be producing renewable diesel for domestic road-fuel consumption and associated RIN generation.

As SAF markets continue to develop, the relationship between renewable diesel capacity, SAF production, exports, and domestic compliance supply will become increasingly important to monitor.

The Market Is More Than Just US Production Capacity

The US renewable diesel industry has the economics needed to run hard:

Diesel prices are elevated

Margins remain strong

LCFS values are improving

Domestic biomass-based diesel demand remains supported by federal mandates

But those conditions do not automatically translate into maximum domestic supply.

Producers now operate within a much broader market in which the same production capacity can potentially serve West Coast compliance markets, international buyers, SAF demand, or conventional domestic renewable diesel consumption.

That means the key question for the remainder of the year may not simply be how much renewable diesel the United States can produce. It may be how much of that production actually stays in the US market and generates the RINs needed to satisfy mandated demand.

With refinery constraints, geopolitical uncertainty, export economics, SAF growth, and changing incentive values all competing for influence, that balance could prove critical heading into the fourth quarter.

Renewable diesel is only one part of a fast-moving biofuels market shaped by shifting feedstock economics, policy, trade flows, and geopolitical risk.

To get a better handle on the market, please join ResourceWise on September 3 at 10:00 AM ET for our Biofuels Market Outlook: Q4 2026 webinar.

Matthew Stone will break down the key developments influencing pricing, feedstocks, policy, SAF, marine biofuels, and global market dynamics heading into the final quarter of the year.

KBR has secured a contract from KMG-Aero and KazFoodProducts for Kazakhstan's first sustainable aviation fuel plant. The deal covers licensing of PureSAF technology and proprietary engineering design using an alcohol-to-jet route. The project is intended to use domestic agricultural feedstocks in low-carbon fuel value chains, aligned with Kazakhstan's aviation hub ambitions.

The project holds significant strategic importance as it supports the President of Kazakhstan’s directive to transform the country into an international aviation hub with strong transit potential. It will also enable the integration of domestically produced agricultural feedstocks into high-value, low-carbon fuel production value chains.

“We are honored to support KMG-Aero and KFP in advancing the national commitment to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, recognizing the pivotal role of aviation decarbonization in achieving these strategic objectives,” said Jay Ibrahim, President, KBR Sustainable Technology Solutions. “KBR’s PureSAF is a feed‑flexible, bankable technology that is designed to deliver high SAF yields and supports the project across the full lifecycle. We look forward to closely collaborating and supporting the successful execution of this landmark SAF project.”

This award builds on other recent PureSAF project wins, reinforcing KBR’s position at the forefront of aviation decarbonization through continued process innovation and low-carbon technology deployment.

text:
A European Union funded project to produce climate-friendly aviation fuel made from tomato plant waste is underway, with scientists across the continent joining efforts to reduce the carbon footprint of the world's highly polluting air traffic.

"These are tomato stalks and stems and we used them for our extraction," chemical engineer Sebastian Sandner tells CGTN while extracting fatty compounds from tomato plant residues - which could be the first step towards the world's most sustainable aviation fuel, often referred to as SAF.

While more and more cars are powered by electricity, airplanes still rely on liquid fuels.

"We will not fly with batteries, that's a vision that is probably relevant in 100 years, but not in the next 50 years," project leader Marlene Kienberger explains.

Aviation is one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize with sustainable fuels accounting for just 0.1 percent per cent of the market. Experts say far more policy support and investment is needed, if there is to be any significant progress towards wider net zero goals.

Currently, aviation biofuel is made from corn or sugarcane which - according to critics - occupies fertile land that could be better used for food production. This is why Kienberger decided to work with farms to use the organic waste from tomato crops which would otherwise be thrown away.

"That includes seeds, that includes the shells, any residues that actually are not of value today we want to turn them into sustainable aviation fuels within this project."

Technically a fruit, tomatoes are the second most consumed vegetable in the world after potatoes and the EU is the third largest producer with around 17 megatonnes of tomatoes harvested.

Their production produces large quantities of residual biomass – plant material such as flowers, leaves and stems, peel and seeds, most of which is currently incinerated as agricultural waste or disposed of at high cost.

Eleven scientific institutions from seven European countries are taking part in the $4 million ToFuel project which in addition to creating sustainable aviation fuel, will produce fertilizer, animal feed and nutritional oil. The technical university in the Austrian city of Graz serves as the main project hub.

The process involves first heating and pressurizing biomass, breaking it down into its cellular components by an abrupt drop in pressure. The subsequent digested biomass sees microorganisms produce lipids that are later processed into aviation fuel.

The subsequent fractionation, biotechnological and purification processes are being developed by the Laboratório Nacional de Energia e Geologia (LNEG) in Lisbon, TU Graz and the University of Zagreb.

"The technologies and the process overall that we are kind of developing within this project need to be robust, so that we can also transfer it to other biobased raw materials," Kienberger explains.

Sourced from tomatoes or other biomass, Kienberger and her international team have four years to create a biofuel and explore the best way to produce it effectively and cost efficiently on an industrial scale. It's giving hope that this red source of fuel… could one day power a green revolution in the skies.

text:
In a study published in ACS Catalysis, an international team that included Dr. Christopher Parlett, Xinyue Zhou, and Yutao Jiang from the Department of Chemical Engineering developed a highly efficient "single-atom catalyst." The researchers also determined, at the molecular level, how the catalyst breaks the strong chemical bonds that help hold lignin together.

The catalyst contains individual ruthenium atoms embedded within a nitrogen-doped carbon material. By keeping the ruthenium atoms isolated, the design can deliver strong catalytic performance while requiring only very small amounts of metal, improving efficiency compared with conventional systems.

Revealing How the Catalyst Breaks Down Lignin

One persistent obstacle in lignin research has been identifying exactly which parts of a catalyst are responsible for breaking the material's unusually strong chemical bonds. Without that information, researchers have had limited guidance for designing more effective catalysts.

The team found that a particular atomic arrangement known as a "Ru-N4 site" is especially important. These sites activate oxygen molecules and help trigger the breaking of both carbon-oxygen and carbon-carbon bonds within lignin.

Using a combination of laboratory experiments and computational modeling, the researchers were able to reconstruct the process in greater detail. The catalyst first activates oxygen, producing highly reactive species. Those species then attack the lignin structure and split it into smaller molecules.

High Conversion With Milder Conditions

When tested under optimized conditions, the catalyst converted nearly all of the model lignin compounds and generated high yields of valuable chemical products, including phenol.

The process also works under relatively mild conditions and does not require harsh chemicals. That combination could make the approach useful for developing more sustainable methods of chemical manufacturing.

The researchers went beyond simplified model compounds and tested the catalyst on real lignin collected from several biomass sources. It successfully converted those samples into useful aromatic compounds that could potentially become building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

A Potential Path Toward Biomass-Based Chemicals

The findings provide a more detailed picture of how single-atom catalysts operate during biomass conversion. That understanding could serve as a guide for developing more efficient catalytic systems in the future.

"Understanding exactly how these catalysts work at the atomic level allows us to design better materials for converting renewable resources into valuable chemicals," said Dr. Christopher Parlett, Lecturer in Chemical Engineering.

By making it easier to upgrade lignin and convert it into higher-value products, the research could support a broader shift away from traditional linear petroleum-derived chemical production and toward a more circular, biomass-based economy.

text:
The Australian Defence Force (ADF) has begun rolling out low carbon liquid fuel (LCLF) blends across its network, with the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) among the early adopters as part of a broader push to strengthen the country’s fuel resilience.

The initiative introduces aviation and diesel fuels containing synthetic components at fuel installations nationwide and aligns with Australia’s 2026 National Defence Strategy, which prioritizes energy security and operational readiness.

RAAF Base East Sale already running on blended fuel

RAAF Base East Sale is already using blended fuel, alongside the Army Aviation Training Centre, and all Australian Defence Force aviation assets are now certified to operate on LCLF, according to the Defence Energy Transition Office (DETO).

That certification work included demonstrations during Exercise Talisman Sabre and the Avalon Air Show, where sustainable aviation fuel was tested on operational platforms.

Officials cite energy security, sovereign fuel production

Brigadier Mark Baldock, Director General Fuel Capability, said diversifying fuel sources is essential to strengthening Defence’s energy security.

He said supporting domestic renewable fuel production also bolsters Australia’s sovereign capability, calling the recent demonstrations an important step toward a more resilient and sustainable energy future for Defence.

Commander Steve Cole, a policy adviser at DETO, said adopting LCLF was becoming inevitable as Australia moves toward greater self-sufficiency. He said DETO’s focus has been ensuring Defence is ready to use these fuels as they become more widely available.

Low carbon liquid fuels are produced from sources other than crude oil, including canola oil, sugar cane, waste oils, and forestry residue. Because they are chemically indistinguishable from fossil fuels, they can be used as drop-in replacements without requiring modifications to existing ADF aircraft or equipment.

Cole said much of the demonstration process has focused on helping maintainers, aircrews, planners, and decision-makers understand that these fuels meet the same specifications as conventional fuel, rather than requiring separate handling or infrastructure.

ADF completes aviation, land certification; sea platforms next

DETO has since shifted focus to formal certification across ADF platforms, a process designed to satisfy internal assurance requirements while also supporting interoperability with partner nations that are adopting similar low carbon fuels.

Beyond aviation, all ADF land assets are also now certified to operate on LCLF, with the Army Aviation Training Centre already using blended fuel. Certification of the remaining maritime platforms is nearing completion.

To support this transition, Defence has established the Defence Fuels Qualification Center in partnership with the Defence Science and Technology Group. The center will focus on promoting fuel standards awareness, conducting qualification testing, and strengthening collaboration with industry to help build sovereign fuel production capacity in Australia.

Negative Emission Technologies Market Summary

The global negative emission technologies market size was valued at USD 1.0 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 1.4 billion in 2026 to USD 7.7 billion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 27.6% from 2026 to 2033. North America dominated the global market, accounting for the largest revenue share of 41.8% in 2025. Negative Emission Technologies are carbon removal solutions that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere or biogenic sources.

They help achieve net-zero emissions by reducing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations through biological, chemical, or engineered carbon removal processes.

Market Dynamics

The Negative Emission Technologies (NETs) market is driven by growing global net-zero commitments, increasing carbon pricing mechanisms, and rising investments in carbon dioxide removal solutions. Government incentives, voluntary carbon markets, and corporate demand for high-quality carbon removal credits are accelerating technology deployment and commercialization. However, high capital costs, technological scalability challenges, and evolving regulatory frameworks continue to restrain market growth. Ongoing advancements in carbon capture, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, direct air capture, and nature-based solutions are expected to create significant growth opportunities over the coming years.

Analyst Perspective

The Negative Emission Technologies (NETs) market is transitioning from pilot-scale projects to early commercial deployment, driven by tightening climate regulations, corporate net-zero commitments, and growing demand for durable carbon removal. An emerging trend is the rise of long-term carbon removal offtake agreements, enabling developers to secure predictable revenue streams and attract project financing before facilities become operational. Certification standards and MRV (Measurement, Reporting, and Verification) frameworks are becoming key differentiators, increasing buyer confidence and supporting premium pricing for high-integrity carbon removal credits. Over the long term, companies that can reduce capture costs, scale operations, and demonstrate verified permanence are expected to strengthen their market position and capture a larger share of the rapidly evolving carbon removal ecosystem.

Technology Insights

The Biochar segment held the largest revenue share of 40.8% in 2025, driven by increasing investments in large-scale carbon removal projects and growing demand for durable CO₂ removal solutions. Biochar offers a relatively mature and scalable pathway for carbon removal, supported by abundant biomass feedstock and applications across agriculture and soil management. Rising corporate net-zero commitments and increasing carbon removal procurement are further supporting the commercial deployment of biochar projects.

The Direct Air Capture (DAC) segment is expected to register the fastest CAGR of 36.6% from 2026 to 2033, driven by increasing demand for scalable and durable CO₂ removal solutions. DAC enables direct removal of CO₂ from ambient air and offers potential for deployment near suitable storage or utilization infrastructure. Growing demand for durable carbon removal credits, corporate net-zero commitments, and increasing investments in emerging CDR technologies are expected to support segment growth.

End Use Insights

The energy & utilities segment held the largest share of 20.54% in 2025, driven by increasing adoption of carbon dioxide removal solutions across power generation and energy infrastructure. Growing pressure to reduce emissions from energy-intensive operations is encouraging utilities to integrate carbon removal with renewable energy and broader decarbonization initiatives. Rising net-zero commitments and investments in low-carbon energy systems are expected to further support segment growth.

The technology & data centers segment is anticipated to register the fastest CAGR of 33.5% during the forecast period. Growth is driven by the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure and increasing electricity consumption associated with AI, cloud computing, and digital services. As technology companies and data center operators pursue net-zero targets, demand for high-quality and durable carbon dioxide removal solutions is increasing. Growing corporate commitments to address residual emissions are expected to accelerate the adoption of carbon removal solutions across the segment.

Regional Insights

North America has emerged as a leading market for negative emission technologies, supported by ambitious net-zero targets, federal incentives, and increasing investments in engineered carbon removal projects. The region is witnessing growing commercialization of direct air capture and BECCS, supported by policy mechanisms, carbon removal initiatives, and rising corporate demand for high-quality carbon removal credits. For instance, in 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy continued advancing its Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs, supporting the development and commercialization of large-scale DAC facilities across the country.

U.S. Negative Emission Technology Market Trends

The U.S. market is witnessing strong growth, driven by supportive federal policies, increasing public and private investments, and rising demand for durable carbon removal solutions. The country benefits from advanced research capabilities, well-developed CO₂ transport and storage infrastructure, and a strong pipeline of commercial-scale projects. Continued government funding, favorable regulatory support, and collaboration between industry and research institutions are expected to accelerate market growth and strengthen the country's leadership in carbon removal.

Europe Negative Emission Technology Market Trends

Europe is a key market for negative emission technologies, driven by strong climate policies, increasing investments, and the development of carbon removal projects. The region has supportive regulatory frameworks, established carbon markets, and growing corporate demand for durable carbon removal solutions, supporting the commercialization of DAC, BECCS, and other CDR technologies. For instance, in 2025, the European Commission advanced its policy framework for permanent carbon removals and carbon farming under the EU Carbon Removal Certification Framework (CRCF), supporting the development and scaling of certified carbon removal activities across Europe.

The UK negative emission technologies market is witnessing steady growth, supported by the country's legally binding net-zero target, strong government commitment to carbon capture and storage, and increasing investments in engineered carbon removal technologies. The UK is developing a robust policy and regulatory framework, including greenhouse gas removal business models and revenue support mechanisms, to encourage private investment and accelerate commercial deployment. These initiatives, combined with expanding carbon storage infrastructure and innovation funding, are strengthening the UK's position as a key market for scalable carbon removal solutions.

Asia Pacific Negative Emission Technology Market Trends

The Asia Pacific market is emerging as a high-growth region, driven by increasing net-zero commitments, rising investments in carbon management, and expanding government support for low-carbon technologies. Countries such as China, Japan, South Korea, and Australia are accelerating carbon removal initiatives through supportive policies and industrial decarbonization efforts. For instance, Japan's Green Innovation Fund, managed by METI and NEDO, provides long-term funding of up to 10 years for projects focused on CO₂ capture, carbon recycling, and carbon absorption technologies, supporting the commercialization of carbon removal solutions across the country.

Latin America Negative Emission Technology Market Trends

The Latin America market is gradually expanding, driven by growing climate commitments, abundant natural carbon sinks, and increasing interest in carbon removal and sustainable land management projects. Countries such as Brazil and Argentina are promoting carbon capture initiatives and nature-based carbon removal through supportive policies and international partnerships. Rising investments in carbon markets and climate finance are expected to accelerate project development and strengthen the region's role in global carbon removal efforts.

Middle East & Africa Negative Emission Technology Market Trends

The Middle East & Africa market is gaining momentum as governments increase investments in carbon management and low-carbon development to support long-term climate goals. Countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia are advancing carbon capture projects, supported by national sustainability strategies and growing public-private partnerships. Rising investments in industrial decarbonization, carbon storage infrastructure, and clean energy initiatives are expected to drive market growth across the region.

Key Negative Emission Technologies Company Insights

Some of the key players operating in the global negative emission technologies market include Climeworks and Charm Industrial, among others.

Climeworks is a leading company in the negative emission technologies market, specializing in DAC solutions that permanently remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The company designs and operates modular DAC plants that capture atmospheric CO₂ for permanent geological storage or sustainable utilization. Climeworks focuses on technology innovation, scalable deployment, and verified carbon removal services to help businesses and governments achieve net-zero targets. Its commercial-scale projects, strategic partnerships, and global presence position the company as a key participant in the global negative emission technologies market.

Charm Industrial is a key player in the negative emission technologies market, specializing in biomass-based carbon removal by converting agricultural and forestry waste into stable bio-oil for permanent underground storage. The company provides durable carbon removal solutions while utilizing low-value biomass that would otherwise release carbon back into the atmosphere. Charm Industrial focuses on scalable operations, long-term carbon storage, and verified carbon removal credits to support corporate decarbonization strategies. Its innovative approach to biomass carbon sequestration and growing portfolio of carbon removal agreements position it as an important participant in the global negative emission technologies market.

text:
KBR has secured a contract from KazMunayGas-Aero LLP (KMG-Aero), a subsidiary of NC KazMunayGas JSC, and KazFoodProducts (KFP) to support the development of Kazakhstan’s first Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) production facility. The project represents a major step toward establishing a domestic SAF industry while strengthening Kazakhstan’s ambitions to become an international aviation and transit hub.

Under the agreement, KBR will license its PureSAF® technology and provide proprietary engineering design services for the planned facility. The PureSAF technology was invented and developed by Swedish Biofuels AB and is based on the alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) pathway. This process enables the conversion of alcohol-based feedstocks into sustainable aviation fuel, providing an alternative to conventional petroleum-derived jet fuel.

The project is strategically aligned with Kazakhstan’s national objective of expanding its role in global aviation. By developing domestic SAF production capabilities, the country can support the aviation sector’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while improving the sustainability of fuel supply chains.

A key feature of the project will be the use of domestically available agricultural feedstocks. These resources can be integrated into higher-value, low-carbon fuel production chains, potentially creating additional value for Kazakhstan’s agricultural sector. The approach could also improve feedstock diversification for SAF production and reduce reliance on conventional fossil-based aviation fuels.

KBR said its PureSAF technology is designed to accommodate a broad range of feedstocks while delivering high SAF yields. The technology is also intended to provide a commercially viable and scalable solution, allowing the project to receive support throughout its development and operational lifecycle.

Jay Ibrahim, President of KBR Sustainable Technology Solutions, said the company is pleased to support KMG-Aero and KFP in advancing Kazakhstan’s commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. He highlighted aviation decarbonization as an important component of the country’s broader sustainability objectives.

The contract also strengthens KBR’s position in the rapidly developing SAF technology market. The award follows other recent PureSAF project wins and demonstrates continued industry interest in alcohol-to-jet technology as governments and airlines pursue lower-carbon aviation fuels.

For Kazakhstan, the facility could establish an important domestic source of sustainable aviation fuel while supporting agricultural value chains, aviation-sector growth and national emissions-reduction objectives. For KBR, the project further expands its portfolio of low-carbon technology deployments and strengthens its presence in the global aviation decarbonization market.

text:
On the map of the chemical industry in Shenze County, a heavyweight chess piece is about to fall. Recently, the Shijiazhuang Administrative Approval Bureau released a public announcement of the acceptance status, and Zhongneng Yida (Hebei) New Energy Co., Ltd.'s new 400000 tons/year sustainable aviation fuel hydrogenation project has officially entered the public announcement process. This means that a green energy factory that uses "urban waste" such as gutter oil and meal waste oil as raw materials is one step closer to breaking ground.

Project scale and construction content

The project is located at No. 22 Xingze Road, Southern District, Shenze Economic Development Zone, Hebei Province, with a total investment of 1853.88 million yuan, including an environmental protection investment of 203.955 million yuan, accounting for 11.0% of the total investment. The project covers an area of approximately 230 acres with a total construction area of 24420 square meters. A 400000 ton/year sustainable aviation fuel hydrogenation unit will be built in the production area, equipped with a 30000 standard cubic meter/hour hydrogen production unit, a 12 ton/hour acidic water stripping unit, as well as emergency response tanks, raw material tank groups, product tank groups and other public auxiliary facilities. The office area is planned to include comprehensive buildings, security guards, and other structures, while implementing outdoor projects such as road hardening, greening, and fence gates simultaneously.

The construction period of the project is about 18 months, and it was registered on October 16, 2025 with the registration number Shen Jing Kai Investment Bei Zi [2025] No. 30.

Raw material sources and product routes

Unlike traditional petroleum refining projects, the "rations" of this factory are pre treated gutter oil, acidified oil, meal waste oil, animal and plant waste oils, and a generation of biodiesel. These raw materials undergo hydrogenation deoxygenation, hydrogenation isomerization, and hydrogenation cracking reactions to ultimately produce three types of products: bio aviation kerosene, bio naphtha, and bio diesel.

The project has designed two production conditions: producing bio aviation kerosene and bio naphtha under SAF conditions, and producing bio diesel and bio naphtha under HVO conditions. Two operating conditions share the same hydrogenation unit, and when switching, only the reaction temperature of the hydrocracking section needs to be adjusted, without generating additional wastewater or solid waste. The desulfurization dry gas generated during the process is used as fuel, while the liquefied gas is sent to the hydrogen production unit to achieve the cascade utilization of materials.

In terms of raw material supply, there are multiple waste oil processing enterprises distributed in the Shenze Economic Development Zone and surrounding counties, which can stably provide industrial oils that meet quality standards, providing strong guarantees for the supply of project raw materials.

Environmental protection supporting facilities and technological highlights

Environmental protection investment exceeding 200 million yuan is a major highlight of this project. The acid water stripping section adopts the chelated iron sulfur process to remove hydrogen sulfide, and the ammonia containing waste gas is sprayed with water to prepare ammonia water. The hydrogen production section purifies hydrogen gas through PSA adsorption to ensure synchronous resource recovery and pollution control.

Against the backdrop of accelerating decarbonization in the global aviation industry, sustainable aviation fuels are seen as one of the key paths to emissions reduction. The International Air Transport Association predicts that by 2050, sustainable fuels such as biofuels will contribute approximately 65% of the aviation industry's carbon emissions reduction. The implementation of the Zhongneng Yida project not only opens up a new channel for the resource utilization of waste oil in the Beijing Tianjin Hebei region, but also adds an important contribution to the large-scale expansion of sustainable aviation fuel production capacity in China.Editor/Yang Meiling

text:

By Chen Aizhu

SINGAPORE, Aug 25 (Reuters) – Hou Qijun has set out to transform Sinopec, the world’s largest refiner, as it faces dwindling fuel demand, overcapacity in petrochemicals and the world’s worst oil crisis, when he could be coasting into retirement like other Chinese state executives.

Appointed as Sinopec chairman a year ago, Hou launched an overhaul to give greater authority to business units ​that he revamped into four profit centres: oil, gas and new energy, refining and chemicals, finance and strategic new business, and a segment ‌combining global trading with Sinopec’s vast marketing teams for fuel, natural gas and chemicals.

He outlined his thinking in unusually blunt language for a state enterprise chief in a government magazine in July.

“The biggest hurdles for such a self-revolutionary transformation lie not on technology, resources or markets, but the system and institutional inertia,” Hou said in the July issue of a publication by China’s powerful State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC).

“As the company grows in scale, its ability to respond to market changes becomes inadequate, and the ‘big company syndrome’ remains to be overcome,” he said.

Sinopec referred ‌to the ​SASAC publication when Reuters sought comment from Hou about his plans to revive the company.

Its fuel sales have ⁠dropped to 2017 levels and it faces an “uphill ⁠battle” to maintain domestic market share, the SASAC magazine said.

An executive with a Chinese institutional investor that owns shares in Sinopec said Hou, at 60, appears to be on a mission to “salvage Sinopec, which has been fighting for survival in a tight spot.”

“Hou is among the few SOE executives who, despite being close to retirement age, is spirited and wants to make some changes,” said the investor, declining to be named due to company policy.

Executives ​at Chinese state firms typically retire at 63.

TOUGH TIMES

On Sunday, Sinopec reported a 19% rise in net profit for the first half of 2026, despite its heavy exposure to oil supply disruptions due to the Iran war and government curbs on passing higher oil prices on to consumers.

Sinopec sold around 3.6 million barrels ⁠per day of gasoline and diesel last year according to company data, mostly at home, ⁠a scale that has become a liability as demand for transport fuels declines with widening vehicle electrification.

“Gasoline was made for ​cars, yet half of new cars no longer need fuel … Under these circumstances, how can producing more gasoline and diesel continue to generate revenue?” Hou said at an ​earnings briefing in Hong Kong on Monday.

“We need to produce more chemical materials instead. In the long run, upstream oil and ‌gas will likewise be replaced by new energy, from high-carbon, to low-carbon, to zero-carbon. Therefore, we must prepare early and develop new energy.”

Sinopec plans to allocate about 20% of its capital spending, or more than 30 billion yuan ($4.46 billion) a year, on new energy and new materials over 2026 to 2030, he said.

In the SASAC report, Hou targeted completion of more than 30 projects by 2030, including growing reserves, producing shale oil, developing sustainable aviation fuel and cutting refining costs.

Such investments focus on “converting ⁠technology into productivity”, he said, calling for “expediting execution”.

The company’s shift to higher-value petrochemicals faces fierce competition from rivals such as local government-backed Wanhua Chemical and privately-led Satellite Chemical as well as overcapacity in ethylene, a key building block in plastics and fiber.

PLAN 2030

In shale, Sinopec is set to start commercial development at the Jiyang ⁠trough, part of its flagship Shengli oilfield, where conventionally-accessible reserves ‌are fast depleting. Hou told reporters in March he was the project’s commander-in-chief.

As a geologist, he built his career ⁠at China’s flagship Daqing oilfield and was general manager of Asia’s largest oil and gas producer, China National Petroleum ​Corp (CNPC), before moving ‌to Sinopec in June 2025.

The Shandong native established his restructuring credentials combining the pipeline assets of China’s three ​oil majors into ⁠a new state firm, PipeChina, which he ran from 2019 to 2021.

A company official described Hou as a “decisive, quick-in-action” workaholic who can speak “off-script for half an hour with conviction and logic”.

With his experience at CNPC and PipeChina, he has a good grasp of the whole energy value chain and could capitalise on government backing for commercially challenging investments such as hydrogen and carbon capture, said Michal Meidan, director of the China program at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.

“The question is how will Sinopec (and its peers) compete with the non-state actors in the new energy space,” she said.

($1 = 6.7238 Chinese yuan renminbi)

(Reporting by Chen Aizhu; Additional reporting by Sam Li and Alison Lui; ​Editing by Tony Munroe and Sonali Paul)

title: Nova Pangaea Technologies completes waste biomass SAF trial - Bioenergy Insight
description:
Nova Pangaea's process converts waste biomass — sawdust, wheat straw and similar residues — into aviation fuel precursors through chemical processing.
The demonstration operates under Project Speedbird, a UK government-backed initiative partnering Nova Pangaea, British Airways and LanzaJet to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from domestic waste biomass.

text:
Nova Pangaea Technologies has completed extended endurance trials on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced from waste biomass at its Teesside demonstration plant, achieving continuous stable operation for up to 72 hours with yields exceeding target specifications.

The trial programme targeted a critical gap in SAF production supply chains: scalable feedstock alternatives to used cooking oil. Nova Pangaea's process converts waste biomass — sawdust, wheat straw and similar residues — into aviation fuel precursors through chemical processing.

The demonstration operates under Project Speedbird, a UK government-backed initiative partnering Nova Pangaea, British Airways and LanzaJet to produce carbon-negative aviation fuel from domestic waste biomass.

The project addresses two concurrent pressures on the aviation sector: sustainable fuel availability and feedstock cost escalation as used cooking oil competition intensifies across biofuels markets.

Nova Pangaea remains pre-commercial scale, with no current SAF production volumes at market quantities. However, the company's technical credibility lies in demonstrating process viability for waste biomass feedstocks and achieving consistent yields over extended operational cycles — both prerequisites for investment scaling.

CEO Stewart Stewart noted that the trial's success should strengthen investor confidence and position waste biomass as a plausible SAF feedstock pathway.

He emphasised the domestic supply advantage — UK waste biomass availability represents a renewable resource base currently underutilised in aviation decarbonisation.

The significance of the trial extends beyond fuel volumes. If Nova Pangaea can demonstrate consistent conversion economics from low-cost waste biomass to aviation-grade SAF, the pathway could materially alter SAF supply economics. Currently, SAF production costs remain elevated primarily due to feedstock costs — predominantly used cooking oil prices reflecting global biofuel demand competition.

Partnerships with British Airways and LanzaJet provide Nova Pangaea with industry credibility and offtake visibility that early-stage SAF developers typically lack.

LanzaJet's established ethanol-to-SAF technology, combined with Nova Pangaea's biomass conversion capability, represents a potential integrated value chain from waste material to certified aviation fuel.

The trial result positions waste biomass as a credible SAF feedstock for future scaling — contingent on demonstrating consistent yields, process reliability and cost economics at volumes relevant to commercial aviation demand.

text:
EVA Airways (2618.TW) today (August 25) formally signed a green transport program cooperation agreement with global freight forwarder AIT Worldwide Logistics. The partnership will add sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced by Formosa Petrochemical (6505.TW) to flights departing from Taiwan, and is expected to provide Microsoft with 15,000 tonnes of Scope 3 carbon reduction environmental benefits in the first year, helping reduce the carbon footprint of its cloud device air transportation. This collaboration links four major industries — aviation, logistics, technology, and energy — establishing a low-carbon transport cooperation model.

EVA Air President Sun Chia-ming said that the aviation industry's net-zero transition requires joint commitment from airlines, fuel suppliers, logistics providers, and corporate customers. This partnership not only demonstrates the power of cross-industry cooperation but also proves that when corporate demand and industry resources are connected, the development of the sustainable aviation fuel market can be accelerated. He looks forward to partnering with more stakeholders to make low-carbon air transport the new normal.

AIT Chief Strategy Officer Greg Weigel noted that AIT ships large volumes of high-value air cargo from Taiwan each year, and EVA Airways has long been a key partner supporting AIT's rapid regional growth, with decades of deep mutual trust established between the two companies. By bringing together key customer Microsoft, core airline partner EVA Airways, and Taiwan-based SAF supplier Formosa Petrochemical, the partnership aims to demonstrate SAF's carbon reduction benefits through cross-industry collaboration, drive market development, and encourage more airlines, fuel suppliers, freight forwarders, and corporate customers across the Asia-Pacific region to participate.

Waste Cooking Oil-Based SAF Delivers Approximately 80% Lifecycle Carbon Reduction

The sustainable aviation fuel used in this initiative is produced from waste cooking oil, with both feedstock sourcing and production processes verified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) scheme. Compared with conventional jet fuel, its lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions are approximately 80% lower. The associated carbon reduction benefits will be managed and transferred through internationally recognized mechanisms, providing Microsoft with supply chain decarbonization outcomes that effectively reduce Scope 3 emissions from air cargo operations.

Since 2025, EVA Airways has been routinely adding SAF to flights departing from Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and has signed a five-year procurement agreement with Formosa Petrochemical. The company stated that as global corporate supply chain decarbonization demand rises, it will continue to help corporate customers and freight forwarders reduce Scope 3 emissions through its green transport program and expand the scale of SAF adoption.

EVA Airways has participated in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) since 2021, has been included in the Sustainability Yearbook for five consecutive years, and in the Dow Jones leading index selection announced in May, became the only Taiwanese airline selected as a constituent of the "DJBIC Emerging Markets Index."

Taiwan's Domestic SAF Supply Remains Tight; Annual Production Only 6,000 Tonnes

Addressing the current SAF supply situation, Formosa Petrochemical President Lin Ko-yen responded that continued investment in relevant facilities is still needed, and expressed hope that the government can assist in securing SAF feedstock and certification, so that corporate customers and willing passengers can participate in net-zero emissions reduction in the future. Based on the contracted purchase volume of 15,000 tonnes, EVA Airways and Microsoft are expected to take several years to complete procurement, primarily because Taiwan's current domestic SAF annual production is only around 6,000 tonnes, and EVA Airways is not the only airline with procurement needs.

Sun Chia-ming also acknowledged that SAF still carries a significant price premium over conventional jet fuel, and that short-term domestic supply remains relatively insufficient. However, he is optimistic that more corporate customers with decarbonization needs will continue to emerge, and that the cooperation model established with AIT and Microsoft will be replicated in the future. He looks forward to continued expansion of the SAF supply chain to support the industry's critical mission of achieving net-zero emissions.

Positive Passenger and Cargo Outlook; AI Servers Drive Cargo Demand

Regarding fourth-quarter operational outlook, EVA Airways assesses that passenger load factors remain solid, though the company continues to monitor spillover effects from earlier conflict-related factors, such as whether conditions on European routes persist. On the cargo side, EVA Airways sees sustained strong demand, with the primary driver being AI server-related shipments. In line with customer requirements, charter services have continued to increase since the second quarter of this year, with overall cargo performance outlook positive.

This four-party collaboration spans an airline, a freight forwarder, a technology company, and an energy supplier. If the cross-industry decarbonization model can be successfully replicated, it will help expand SAF adoption across the Asia-Pacific region. However, with Taiwan's domestic SAF annual production capacity at only approximately 6,000 tonnes against a single partnership requiring 15,000 tonnes, the pace of supply chain expansion will be a key factor to watch going forward.

Techno-Economic Assessment of SMR Nuclear Propulsion for Deep-Sea Bulk Carriers Through AIS-Informed Operational Cost Modelling

Augustin Hazard

Maritime shipping (~3% of global emissions) faces mounting pressure to decarbonise. SMR nuclear propulsion, combining near-zero emissions with low operating costs, offers a compelling pathway. Yet operationally grounded techno-economic assessments of nuclear vessels remain scarce. This project addresses that gap by developing an AIS-informed operational cost model focused on large deep-sea bulk carriers (Capesize+), enabling rigorous comparison between nuclear and conventional vessels across key operational variables. The findings will feed into a parallel project examining the broader macro-economic implications of nuclear shipping, together building a comprehensive picture of whether nuclear propulsion offers a genuine cost advantage.

Verification of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Through (14C) Radiocarbon Analysis of Aerosol Particles

Emily Ran Fan

This project investigates the feasibility of radiocarbon (14C) analysis as an independent method for verifying Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) use at the point of combustion. The experimental component analyses quartz filter-collected aerosol particles from aircraft auxiliary power unit (APU) using accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS), with measured fossil and biogenic carbon contributions compared against known fuel blend ratios. A complementary interview component explores stakeholder perspectives on current SAF verification, certification, market integrity, and the potential role of physical verification methods in SAF supply chains.

Supervisor 1: Professor Marc Stettler, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

Supervisor 2: Dr. Georgia Gamble, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

Modelling the Potential of Cycling and E-Bikes to replace Car Commuting in London

Leo Duhamel-Callot

Transport is the UK's largest source of emissions, and commuting by private vehicle concentrates congestion and pollution in major cities. Bikes and e-bikes could replace many of these journeys, yet no existing framework combines socio-demographic parameters to estimate how many private-vehicle commutes could realistically be shifted to these modes. This project, in collaboration with Energy Systems Catapult, develops a demographically segmented substitution model for London, integrating parameters such as age, gender, income and trip distance. It then evaluates policy scenarios and quantifies the resulting reductions in CO₂ emissions, the health benefits, and the associated cost savings.

Supervisor 1: Christabel Ofori-Atta, Energy Systems Catapult

Supervisor 2: Dr. Ahmadreza Faghih Imani, Centre for Environmental Policy

A Full Financial Viability Assessment of Nuclear Propulsion in Commercial Shipping​

Ong Wui Shuen

This project aims to develop a techno-economic model to assess the financial viability of small modular reactor (SMR) propulsion in commercial shipping. The model combines vessel operational data derived from AIS records with ship specifications, voyage economics, capital costs, operating expenditure and financing assumptions to generate 25-year cashflow projections. Nuclear propulsion is evaluated under three financing structures: (i) Outright SMR purchase, (ii) An SMR lease or service model, and (iii) A government-backed purchase. These scenarios are then compared against a conventional heavy-fuel-oil vessel. Financial performance is assessed using net present value, internal rate of return, simple and discounted payback periods, and break-even freight rates. A subsequent sensitivity analysis is conducted to examine how factors such as SMR capital cost, freight rates, inflation, discount rates and potential improvements in vessel speed affect the commercial competitiveness of nuclear-powered shipping.

The successful flight therefore represents not only a milestone for Heart Aerospace but also a demonstration of the progress being made toward integrating electric propulsion into commercial aircraft architectures.

On the other hand, sustainable aviation fuel is especially important for larger aircraft and longer distance operations because it can be utilized with current aircraft and aviation fuel infrastructure.

Thus, a more comprehensive multi technology approach to aviation decarbonization may benefit from the development of hybrid electric aircraft. Airlines may progressively blend sustainable aviation fuel for aircraft that need more range and payload capacity with electric aircraft for suitable regional routes.

Opportunities in fuel production transportation airport infrastructure storage blending certification and distribution are also created by the ongoing development of sustainable aviation fuel. Sustainable aviation fuel has been increasingly associated in recent industry talks with energy security, fuel supply resilience and emissions reduction.

text:
News from Wellington Airport

Wellington Airport has released its annual Kaitiakitanga report today, showing a 29% drop in gross emissions since 2017 as part of its annual climate and environmental reporting. This includes Scope 1 and 2 emissions and business travel.

When certified renewable energy is included, direct emissions (Scope 1 and 2) have decreased by 77% since 2017. This puts the airport well on track for its target of Net Zero emissions for Scope 1 and 2 by 2030, with the replacement of gas boilers in 2028 expected to bring the total close to 100%.

Wellington Airport chief executive Matt Clarke says the airport has also achieved a 21% reduction in waste to landfill since 2017, on track to meet a target of 30% by 2030.

“We’re proud to be ranked among the most sustainable airports in the world. A key part of this is setting clear goals and publishing regular updates on how we’re tracking.

“Emissions from aircraft themselves are still clearly the biggest challenge, but we are making progress in that area too. Airlines are operating more fuel-efficient aircraft at Wellington, and we proudly hosted Air New Zealand’s first electric aircraft last summer.”

The emissions progress is a highlight of Wellington Airport’s annual Kaitiakitanga report which summarises the airport’s environmental and social efforts.

Other highlights over the past 12 months include:

– Fast-track approval for southern seawall renewal

– Founding member of the New Zealand Sustainable Aviation Fuel Industry Roundtable

– Successful feasibility study paving way for replacement of gas boilers

– Solar panels installed on roof of new Airport Fire Station

– 23% of available seat kilometres operated by next-generation fuel efficient aircraft (compared with 9% in 2020)

– Sponsorship of nearly every major Wellington event and support for local causes including Predator Free Wellington

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel: The Hidden Winner in Electric Vehicle Economics

by Alexei Beltyukov (Universal Fuel Technologies/SAF Magazine) ... More than 98% of U.S. gasoline sold at gas stations contains ethanol, and U.S. gasoline consumption is declining even as miles driven increase. This creates direct pressure on the 14 billion gallons of ethanol produced annually in the United States, primarily for gasoline blending. As EV adoption accelerates, ethanol producers face a market shift as their primary customer base is entering long-term decline.

For SAF, this is an opportunity rather than collateral damage. The automotive transition creates three simultaneous advantages for SAF production.

First, feedstock availability improves. Ethanol producers facing declining gasoline demand have a clear incentive to seek alternative markets. Even redirecting a modest fraction of current production toward jet fuel would significantly increase SAF feedstock availability. More importantly, softening demand creates downward price pressure, improving alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) economics. The threshold at which ethanol-based SAF becomes cost-competitive with conventional jet fuel depends on multiple factors, but ethanol feedstock costs represent the dominant factor in alcohol-to-jet economics. As declining gasoline demand softens ethanol pricing, the pathway toward cost-competitive SAF production becomes increasingly viable.

Second, infrastructure becomes available. Refineries configured for gasoline production face a choice: adapt or confront stranded asset risk, and a number of them have already downsized or shut down. Repurposing equipment for SAF production offers a path to maintain utilization and revenue rather than writing off capital investments. Coprocessing renewable and fossil feedstocks enables a gradual transition, reducing risk while building operational experience. The distributed refinery network can be redirected, rather than constructed.

Third, the market is demanding economic realism. As SAF projects scale and seek federal support through loan guarantees and production credits, investors and government agencies increasingly require transparent cost disclosure and credible projections. Technologies that can leverage existing infrastructure rather than require greenfield construction offer more defensible economics. This shift favors practical pathways over theoretical innovation.

There's an energy security dimension as well. Ethanol-derived fuels would be domestically produced from feedstock to final product. The U.S. already ranks among the world's top ethanol producers, with established supply chains and processing expertise concentrated in the Midwest. Converting this capacity toward aviation fuel would reduce reliance on imported petroleum and vulnerable supply routes.

Why Ethanol-Based Pathways Meet Emerging SAF Requirements

...

As regulations move toward higher SAF blends and eventually 100% fully synthetic fuel, aircraft manufacturers and regulators will require fuels capable of delivering complete performance without fossil blending. This creates a new competitive advantage for technologies capable of producing both paraffinic and aromatic components. Alcohol-based pathways, particularly ethanol-to-jet, offer this flexibility. As ethanol becomes available at a lower cost due to declining gasoline demand, the economic case for ethanol pathways that can produce complete, drop-in-ready fuel strengthens significantly.

title: Europe's Biogas Plants Could Become Fertilizer Factories | OilPrice.com
description:
When gas prices rise, ammonia costs rise, fertilizer plants reduce production, and farmers become exposed to a global commodity chain they cannot control.
Very few ask a more disruptive question: could the gas become fertilizer before it ever leaves the site?
Small Ammonia Is No Longer Only a Laboratory Idea Conventional ammonia plants became enormous for good reason.
Carbon Determines Whether the Product Is Truly Different Biogas contains biogenic carbon, but converting its methane into hydrogen still creates CO2.
For decades, fertilizer production moved toward ever larger plants located near cheap fossil gas.
text:
The fertilizer crisis is usually framed as a natural gas problem. When gas prices rise, ammonia costs rise, fertilizer plants reduce production, and farmers become exposed to a global commodity chain they cannot control.

That diagnosis is correct but incomplete.

Across Europe, thousands of anaerobic digesters are already producing a methane-rich gas close to the farms and food industries that consume fertilizer. Most sites burn it in a combined heat and power unit, upgrade it to biomethane, or flare a small surplus. Very few ask a more disruptive question: could the gas become fertilizer before it ever leaves the site?

At household scale, the answer is no. At the larger end of the biogas market, it is becoming technically plausible.

The real opportunity is not a miniature chemical plant on every farm. It is a new industrial category between the digester and the conventional million-tonne ammonia complex.

The Feedstock Is Already in the Right Place

Raw biogas typically contains roughly 55% to 65% methane, with most of the remainder being carbon dioxide. A plant producing 1,000 normal cubic metres per hour therefore provides around 600 Nm3 of methane per hour before purification.

That is not trivial.

Using standard chemical relationships, this methane stream could theoretically support ammonia production on the order of 25 to 30 tonnes per day, depending on methane content, conversion efficiency, downtime and the treatment of process losses. The exact plant output requires engineering, but the scale is clear: a large digester can sit in the gap between laboratory equipment and conventional centralized production.

The route is familiar. Sulphur and other contaminants are removed. Methane is converted into hydrogen through reforming. Nitrogen is separated from air. Hydrogen and nitrogen then enter an ammonia synthesis loop. The carbon dioxide already present in the raw gas, plus the CO2 created during reforming, must be separated and either used, stored or released.

None of these steps is scientifically novel. The challenge is making them economic and reliable at a scale the ammonia industry has historically avoided.

Small Ammonia Is No Longer Only a Laboratory Idea

Conventional ammonia plants became enormous for good reason. High-temperature reforming, gas purification, compression and Haber-Bosch synthesis benefit from scale. Shrinking the process increases capital cost per tonne and leaves fewer operating hours over which to recover the investment.

But modular ammonia technology has moved below the traditional scale threshold. Proton Ventures has developed decentralized NFuel concepts and is involved in a 4-tonne-per-day green ammonia pilot in Morocco using electrolysis and Haber-Bosch synthesis. Stamicarbon markets ammonia technology starting at 50 tonnes per day, while academic work has examined small-scale ammonia from biomass gasification and biogas.

These examples do not prove that a 1,000 Nm3-per-hour biogas-to-ammonia plant is commercially ready off the shelf. They prove that ammonia synthesis is moving into the scale range where such integration can be seriously engineered.

That distinction matters. Announced concepts are not operating references. A credible project must still demonstrate availability, catalyst performance, maintenance requirements and product quality under real biogas conditions.

The Business Case Is About More Than Gas Price

A decentralized plant will struggle to beat a fully utilized world-scale ammonia facility on pure production cost in normal markets. It does not need to.

Its value comes from combining advantages that centralized production does not have: an existing local feedstock, avoided biomethane-grid infrastructure, reduced fertilizer transport, possible use of process heat, proximity to agricultural customers and lower exposure to international gas shocks.

The comparison also changes if the alternative is not a perfectly efficient global plant, but imported ammonia delivered inland during a volatile market. Farmers buy security as well as molecules.

Still, free or cheap biogas is not enough. The plant needs high annual utilization. Ammonia synthesis does not reward intermittent operation, and a digester with unstable gas quality can create costly downstream problems. Sites must have professional gas cleaning, steady feedstock supply, competent operators and enough local demand to absorb the product.

Safety is equally decisive. Ammonia is toxic, pressurized and regulated. Producing it close to agriculture reduces logistics but transfers industrial responsibility to the site. Modularization must therefore simplify operation without pretending the process is harmless.

Carbon Determines Whether the Product Is Truly Different

Biogas contains biogenic carbon, but converting its methane into hydrogen still creates CO2. If that carbon is simply vented, the ammonia may offer supply-security benefits and potentially lower fossil emissions, yet it is not zero-carbon.

The strongest configuration separates a concentrated biogenic CO2 stream for use or permanent storage. That could make the plant not merely low-carbon but potentially carbon-negative at the system level, depending on feedstock, methane leakage, energy use and storage integrity.

This is where biogas has an advantage over fossil natural gas. The carbon started in the short biological cycle. Capturing and storing it can create a removal, while the hydrogen becomes fertilizer.

But again, the business model must come first. A remote site without affordable CO2 transport or a local user cannot assume carbon revenue. The capture unit may be technically easy compared with the logistics.

Target the Niche Before Claiming a Revolution

The wrong strategy would be to sell decentralized ammonia as a replacement for Europe's fertilizer industry. Large plants will remain more efficient for bulk supply, and many small digesters are far below the required scale.

The right first market is narrower: large agricultural or industrial biogas plants, probably around 750 to 1,500 Nm3 per hour, with clean and stable gas, concentrated nearby fertilizer demand, sufficient grid capacity and a realistic CO2 outlet. Cooperative ownership could aggregate demand and professionalize operation.

Those conditions will exclude many sites. That is a strength, not a weakness. New energy technologies fail when they confuse theoretical addressable volume with investable projects.

Europe does not need thousands of immediate installations. It needs a handful of well-instrumented demonstrations proving output, availability, emissions and delivered fertilizer cost across seasons. If those work, standardized modules can follow.

For decades, fertilizer production moved toward ever larger plants located near cheap fossil gas. Biogas creates the possibility of reversing part of that logic: producing closer to the carbon source, the nutrient cycle and the customer.

The future fertilizer factory may not always sit at a port or gas field.

Some of it may already be bubbling beside the farm.

By Leon Stille for Oilprice.com

text:
Vancouver International Airport (YVR) has announced a new initiative to accelerate the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

YVR’s new online calculator tool allows travellers to estimate their flight’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and contribute to the use of SAF.

What is SAF

A lower-carbon alternative to fossil jet fuel, SAF is made from renewable materials such as municipal solid waste, cooking waste, meat production waste, and agricultural and forestry residues. That means it’s not a fossil fuel and uses carbon already in the biosphere.

SAF emissions are estimated to be 80 per cent lower than fossil jet fuel on a lifecycle basis. SAF also improves air quality by reducing particulate matter and sulphur emissions compared to fossil jet fuel.

The aviation industry is actively working towards achieving net zero by 2050, and SAF will be a key part of achieving it.

Leading the industry’s transition

As the second busiest airport in Canada, it’s a pretty big deal that YVR is committed to reducing emissions from its own operations. But that’s not all; YVR is also stepping into a leadership role to increase SAF usage across the industry.

While SAF has great potential, its supply is limited and costs more than conventional jet fuel. Increasing demand is needed to scale production and increase availability.

As a simple addition to your journey, YVR’s online calculator tool allows travellers to be part of the transition to a lower-carbon aviation industry. You can estimate your flight’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

Collective action like this could help in driving long-term change across the industry!

Sustainability for the future

YVR says it is committed to a sustainable future (just look at its history of innovation), and remains on course to become net zero by 2030. YVR is also committed to supporting all partners in achieving the aviation industry’s broader goal of net zero emissions by 2050.

The patent expansion could become strategically important if American EcoFuels successfully moves its technology toward commercial deployment.

Rather than protecting only an individual fuel or process step, AEFI is seeking to establish a broader intellectual property perimeter around an integrated platform for converting carbon-containing feedstocks into synthesis gas and ultimately into products including SAF, synthetic paraffinic kerosene and clean diesel.

That approach could provide greater flexibility in how the technology is commercialised. The company has identified potential models including its own production facilities, jointly developed projects, strategic partnerships and licensing arrangements.

Licensing may be particularly relevant to the capital requirements of future expansion because, according to the company, it could allow AEFI to participate economically in multiple facilities without independently financing and constructing each plant.

However, the Phase 2 plan remains at an early stage. The contemplated applications still require preparation, legal review and filing, and there is no assurance that all 584 will be submitted or ultimately become issued patents.

The announcement also does not establish commercial revenue from the technology. The value of the expanded patent portfolio will therefore depend partly on AEFI's ability to progress through engineering, testing, certification and eventual commercialisation.

Reporting Milestone Adds Another Near-Term Catalyst

Alongside its intellectual property programme, American EcoFuels said its two-year PCAOB audit is nearing completion.

The company has also substantially advanced its Form 10 registration statement and currently expects to file it with the SEC before the end of the third quarter of 2026, subject to completion of the audit and final legal, accounting and management review.

Completing those steps could strengthen AEFI's reporting framework as management pursues its broader capital markets and commercialisation objectives.

What to Watch Next

Individual patent filings under the Phase 2 programme will provide an indication of how quickly American EcoFuels converts its proposed 584-application strategy into filed intellectual property.

Completion of the PCAOB audit and the targeted third-quarter Form 10 filing represent more immediate corporate milestones.

Beyond those steps, investors may watch for progress in engineering, test-plant operations, fuel testing and certification, strategic partnerships and commercial projects. Those developments will ultimately help determine whether AEFI's expanding intellectual property portfolio translates into commercial value.
